readings.title: Childhood contentment and its hidden costs — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a list of apparent freedoms for the deprivation each one records.
readings.focus: How an adult narrator describes a happy childhood without letting slavery off the hook.
readings.context: Douglass, born in 1818 on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, has described his grandmother’s cabin at Tuckahoe and an “old master” whose power he only dimly felt as a small child. These paragraphs close the first chapter by generalising about the first years of an enslaved boy. Tow-linen is coarse cloth made from flax waste; ablution is washing.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass uses period phrases such as “our sable boy” and “little heathen,” partly in irony.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “The Author's Childhood,” from the quoted verse to the end of the chapter; opens “"The tear down childhood's cheek that flows, Is like the dew-drop on the rose,-- When…”; closes “…boy, so far as I can now remember, was the boy whose life in slavery I am now narrating.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass quotes a verse comparing a child’s tear to dew on a rose. How does the paragraph after it use, and complicate, the verse’s comfort?
facilitatorNotes: The verse says childhood sorrow dries quickly, and Douglass agrees that the neglected slave-child and the petted slaveholder’s child feel about equal contentment, crediting divine mercy. The long paragraph then shows that this contentment rests on neglect and on the master having nothing yet to fear.
evidence: Is like the dew-drop on the rose,--
The spirit of the All Just mercifully holds the balance for the young.

questions.prompt: The long paragraph lists troubles the slave-boy “escapes.” How does each escape also record a deprivation?
facilitatorNotes: No scolding about knife and fork, because he has none; no soiled tablecloth, because he eats on a clay floor; no torn clothes, because he has almost none; little crying, because no one cares. The humour is double-edged, and the reader supplies the cost.
evidence: for he uses none
cries but little, for nobody cares for his crying

questions.prompt: According to the opening sentence, why can the slaveholder “easily afford” to spare small children, and what does that imply about the years ahead?
facilitatorNotes: He has “nothing to fear from impotent childhood”: restraint is calculated, and cruelty is reserved for those who can work or resist. The half-forgotten threat that the boy will “see sights” by-and-by points to what is coming.
evidence: having nothing to fear from impotent childhood
he will be made to "see sights" by-and-by

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass describe his own early childhood as that of “the slave-boy,” in the third person, until the final sentence?
facilitatorNotes: The general description makes the passage testimony about a class of children, not only memoir; the last sentence ties the type to the particular “I.” The distance also lets the adult narrator be ironic about what the child did not yet understand. Readers may also notice how period phrases like “little heathen” sit inside that irony.
evidence: And such a boy, so far as I can now remember, was the boy whose life in slavery I am now narrating.

readings.title: A father in rumour, a mother made a myth — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that reverses the reader’s expectation step by step.
readings.focus: How the law of slavery turned family into property and destroyed filial feeling.
readings.context: Douglass has told of his mother’s rare night visits from a farm twelve miles away and learned only after her death that she could read. These closing paragraphs of Chapter III turn to the father he never knew. The “curse of Ham” was a reading of Genesis 9 that defenders of slavery used to justify enslaving Africans; mulatto was the period term for a person of mixed Black and white parentage.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage concerns slaveholders’ sexual exploitation of enslaved women and the beating of their children, and includes a period generalisation about white Southern wives.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Author's Parentage,” from his mother’s death to the end of the chapter; opens “Summoned away to her account, with the impassable gulf of slavery between us during her…”; closes “…Her grave is, as the grave of the dead at sea, unmarked, and without stone or stake.”.

questions.prompt: What does the law that children “are reduced to the condition of their mothers” have to do with the rumour about Douglass’s father?
facilitatorNotes: Douglass doubts the rumour, but the law is the real fact: a slaveholder’s children by an enslaved woman are his property, so exploitation becomes profitable, adding “profit” to “the pleasure of sin.”
evidence: children, in all cases, are reduced to the condition of their mothers
the additional attraction of profit

questions.prompt: Douglass argues that such children fare worse than other slaves, not better. Trace his reasons.
facilitatorNotes: A man who enslaves his own blood is not magnanimous; the child’s face accuses him; his wife hates the child and has the means to hurt it. So selling the child away can be “an act of humanity.” The argument reverses the reader’s first assumption at each step.
evidence: the mulatto child's face is a standing accusation against him who is master and father to the child
it is often an act of humanity toward the slave-child to be thus removed

questions.prompt: How does Douglass turn the proslavery “curse of Ham” argument against itself?
facilitatorNotes: If only Ham’s descendants may be enslaved, the thousands of children of white fathers make American slavery “unscriptural” by its own defenders’ logic. “The thoughtful know the rest” leaves sexual violence unstated but unmistakable.
evidence: slavery in this country will soon become an unscriptural institution
The thoughtful know the rest.

questions.prompt: Douglass admits he felt “no strong emotions of sorrow” at his mother’s death. How does he keep the reader from censuring him?
facilitatorNotes: He lays the absence of feeling at slavery’s door: it made siblings strangers and turned his mother into a myth. He learned her value later by watching other mothers. The unmarked grave “as the grave of the dead at sea” completes the loss. Many readers find this honesty more moving than conventional grief.
evidence: There is not, beneath the sky, an enemy to filial affection so destructive as slavery.
unmarked, and without stone or stake.

readings.title: Uncle Isaac’s prayers and the windmill — excerpt
readings.challenge: Hear when Douglass’s humour turns into argument.
readings.focus: Manners, names and the whip among the enslaved people of the home plantation.
readings.context: Douglass, about seven, has been brought to Colonel Lloyd’s great plantation on the Wye River, where his owner, Captain Anthony, manages Lloyd’s farms. The previous paragraphs described its many workshops and dwellings; the “mechanics” are its skilled workers. Hickory switches are flexible sticks used for whipping.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Children are whipped during prayer lessons; Douglass offers a period generalisation about “my race” and uses the word “darkey.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “A General Survey of the Slave Plantation,” from the plantation “uncles” to the old master’s indifference; opens “These mechanics were called "uncles" by all the younger slaves, not because they really…”; closes “…of my advent, as he would have thought of the addition of a single pig to his stock!”.

questions.prompt: Douglass explains the title “uncle” and says good manners are strictly enforced among the enslaved. What double point does he make about respect?
facilitatorNotes: Elders receive rigid respect, and the enslaved demand from one another the respect they are compelled to show masters: dignity kept up under subjection, and a mirror of the master’s demands. His explanation that it is “partly constitutional with my race” reflects period thinking; separate the observation from the generalisation.
evidence: He shows to others, and exacts for himself, all the tokens of respect which he is compelled to manifest toward his master.

questions.prompt: What does Douglass’s remark about surnames reveal about the North as well as the South?
facilitatorNotes: Even abolitionists rarely grant a Black man a surname; formal first names replace nicknames, but equal address “goes against the grain.” Isaac Copper’s surname is an exception that had to be held against convention. Douglass criticises his own allies.
evidence: even abolitionists make very little of the surname of a negro
It goes against the grain to treat and address a negro precisely as they would treat and address a white man.

questions.prompt: How is the scene of Uncle Isaac’s prayer lesson both comic and an argument?
facilitatorNotes: The comedy: a “doctor of divinity” whose remedies are salts, castor oil, the Lord’s Prayer and switches, and a lecture on consequences “especially those more immediate.” The argument: the whip pervades even relations among the enslaved and spoils devotion. Douglass admits he was “often a truant.”
evidence: for those of the soul, the Lord's Prayer, and hickory switches!
Everybody, in the south, wants the privilege of whipping somebody else.

questions.prompt: Why did the boy come to “think very highly” of the plantation, and why did the old master lose his terrors?
facilitatorNotes: The windmill, the boats bound for Baltimore, and fish and oysters for the taking made it a field for enterprise. The old master simply ignored him, as he would ignore one more pig. The relief rests on being treated as livestock, and the exclamation mark carries the adult’s irony.
evidence: I began to think very highly of Col. L.'s plantation
the addition of a single pig to his stock!

readings.title: Aunt Katy, hunger and plantation rank — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of delegated power down to the child at the bottom of it.
readings.focus: Hunger, favouritism and rank in the household that held the young Douglass.
readings.context: Recap: on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation the boy found a strict code of manners, a lame prayer-teacher who used the switch, and a windmill and passing boats that delighted him; his owner, Captain Anthony, hardly noticed him. A butler here is the plantation’s chief manager of stores; a cooper makes barrels.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Includes a mother wounding her son with a knife, a child’s hunger, the yearly sale of an enslaved person, and Douglass’s dismissive judgment of African-born people’s speech.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “A General Survey of the Slave Plantation,” from Captain Anthony’s duties to the end of the chapter; opens “As the chief butler on Col. Lloyd's plantation, his duties were numerous and perplexing.…”; closes “…received; of which impressions you will learn more in the coming chapters of this book.”.

questions.prompt: How does the account of Captain Anthony’s duties explain why the children were handled “in classes or sizes”?
facilitatorNotes: He holds the keys, measures allowances, ships the produce and oversees the shops, so he has no time for children. As Lloyd delegates to him, he delegates to Aunt Katy, and the children receive power at the end of that chain.
evidence: What he was to Col. Lloyd, he made Aunt Katy to him.
disposing of us in classes or sizes

questions.prompt: How does Douglass judge Aunt Katy, and how fairly does he try to do it?
facilitatorNotes: He calls her ambitious, ill-tempered and cruel, and tells of the knife and the starved children. Yet he grants her industry and some “maternal feeling,” and notes she was the only mother allowed to keep her children, a favour that depended on pleasing old master. The system rewards her cruelty.
evidence: she was the only mother who was permitted to retain her children around her
it is not to accuse her too severely

questions.prompt: What do the particular details of the boy’s hunger make a reader see that a general statement could not?
facilitatorNotes: Fighting the dog for crumbs, following the girl who shakes the tablecloth, prizing meat-water and rusty bacon rind: hunger becomes concrete and humiliating. The old slaves’ “better day comin’” is set beside it as real consolation.
evidence: I have fought with the dog--"Old Nep"--for the smallest crumbs
the skin taken from rusty bacon, was a positive luxury

questions.prompt: Captain Anthony’s yearly sale of one person is called a “crop,” and the chapter closes on “rank and station.” What picture of the plantation’s values do these details give?
facilitatorNotes: People are produce, harvested at seven or eight hundred dollars a year, and every household keeps its distance from the one above it. The flat, bookkeeping tone of “crop” makes the sale more chilling than outrage would.
evidence: This crop, therefore, brought him seven or eight hundred dollars a year
The idea of rank and station was rigidly maintained on Col. Lloyd's plantation.

questions.prompt: Douglass calls the speech of African-born people “broken,” yet says that “Color makes no difference with a child.” How should a reader weigh his judgment of their speech?
facilitatorNotes: He writes as a self-educated man who prizes standard English and blames the plantation’s isolation for his lack of learning; “so far as they had ideas” is condescending, and readers should examine it rather than accept it. His point about children playing across colour lines asserts a natural equality that his judgment of adult speech does not extend.
evidence: so broken was their speech
Color makes no difference with a child.

readings.title: A master explained by the system — excerpt
readings.challenge: Distinguish the child’s expectations from the adult narrator’s explanation of them.
readings.focus: Slavery as a system that shapes character, and the slave’s calculated use of appeal.
readings.context: Douglass’s owner, Captain Anthony, at first gave the boy little attention. This chapter turns to what the child gradually learned about him. An overseer managed enslaved workers in the fields for the owner; “bowels of compassion” is a biblical phrase for pity.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes a drunken overseer’s beating of a young woman and her master’s refusal to protect her.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Gradual Initiation into the Mysteries of Slavery,” from the opening to the policy of appealing against an overseer; opens “ALTHOUGH my old master--Capt. Anthony--gave me at first, (as the reader will have already…”; closes “…the rigor of his rule, after an outbreak of the kind to which I have been referring.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes that “The slaveholder, as well as the slave, is the victim of the slave system.” What evidence does he give, and does it excuse Captain Anthony?
facilitatorNotes: In a free state, under just restraints, Anthony might have been as humane as anyone; character takes its shape from surroundings, and under slavery reason is imprisoned while passion runs like prairie fire. The explanation does not erase the “outrages, deep, dark and nameless.” Readers may debate whether explaining cruelty this way lessens personal responsibility.
evidence: The slaveholder, as well as the slave, is the victim of the slave system.
A man's character greatly takes its hue and shape from the form and color of things about him.

questions.prompt: What did the child learn by watching his master mutter to himself, and what general claim does Douglass build on it?
facilitatorNotes: The master ignored the children as he ignored ducks and geese, but the boy understood him. Douglass generalises: masters underrate the enslaved, and the enslaved let them believe their ignorance is real. Both sides practise a kind of deception.
evidence: Slaveholders ever underrate the intelligence with which they have to grapple.
the slave is cunning enough to make the master think he succeeds

questions.prompt: What did the boy expect when his beaten cousin came for protection, and how does the adult narrator explain what happened instead?
facilitatorNotes: He expected rage at the overseer; the master sent her back with a threat. The adult explains it as “part of the system, rather than a part of the man”: hearing complaints would undermine overseers and make the master his own overseer.
evidence: I expected to see him boil over with rage
This treatment is a part of the system, rather than a part of the man.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass say that a slave who appeals is often vindicated “in the end”? What does this show about resistance under slavery?
facilitatorNotes: Even if beaten for it, the complainer usually finds the overseer more careful afterwards, so appeal is a long-term strategy that requires “nerve.” Resistance works through calculated risk rather than immediate relief.
evidence: when a slave has nerve enough to exercise it
in the end the policy of complaining is, generally, vindicated

readings.title: Esther and the master’s passion — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice what a child witness can see, and what an adult narrator chooses to withhold.
readings.focus: The difference between cruelty as policy and cruelty as passion, and slavery’s denial of marriage.
readings.context: Recap: Douglass has explained Captain Anthony’s refusal to protect a cousin beaten by an overseer as the policy of the system rather than the cruelty of the man, and noted that bold appeals sometimes curb an overseer in the end. Esther was Douglass’s aunt; a cowskin is a heavy whip.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes in detail a master’s whipping of a young woman, with a sexual motive implied, witnessed by the narrator as a child.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Gradual Initiation into the Mysteries of Slavery,” from the slaveholder’s wrath to the end of the chapter; opens “Howsoever the slaveholder may allow himself to act toward his slave, and, whatever…”; closes “…repeated in the case of poor Esther, and her life, as I knew it, was one of wretchedness.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first paragraph distinguish the master’s policy from his passion, and why is his wrath worse than an overseer’s?
facilitatorNotes: Refusing redress is policy; when his own passions are roused he is “irresponsible,” checked only by profit and loss. The overseer acts mechanically; the master acts “with a will.”
evidence: What may have been mechanically and heartlessly done by the overseer, is now done with a will.
except in so far as it may concern profit or loss

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass call personal beauty “a curse to the slave-girl”?
facilitatorNotes: Beauty draws the owner’s desire, and the law gives her no protection: Anthony breaks up a courtship from motives Douglass calls “abhorrent.” Without recognised marriage, an enslaved woman is at the mercy of her owner’s power and caprice.
evidence: that which is ever a curse to the slave-girl; namely,--personal beauty
a slave-woman is at the mercy of the power, caprice and passion of her owner

questions.prompt: Douglass watched through the cracks of a closet. How does that position shape what he tells and what he withholds?
facilitatorNotes: He is a hidden, helpless child who sees and hears without being seen. He reports Esther’s own cry but refuses to reproduce the master’s words; the restraint gives the account authority. His fear, that her fate “might be mine next,” is part of the testimony.
evidence: through the cracks of its unplaned boards
His answers to them are too coarse and blasphemous to be produced here.

questions.prompt: Before telling Esther’s story, Douglass insists that such events are “not singular nor isolated.” Why does he need that claim?
facilitatorNotes: It prevents readers from treating the scene as an aberration and makes it evidence about the system, in line with his argument that slavery shapes every master. Readers can ask how far one witness can support a general claim, and what else in the book supports it.
evidence: are not singular nor isolated in slave life, but are common in every slaveholding community in which I have lived

readings.title: Why am I a slave? — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate a child’s questions from the adult narrator’s conclusions.
readings.focus: A child’s reasoning against the religious and racial justifications of slavery.
readings.context: After witnessing his aunt Esther’s whipping, Douglass, then about seven or eight, began to question slavery itself. “Guinea” was a general name for the West African coast.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Recalls the whipping of the narrator’s aunt and the kidnapping of Africans into slavery.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Treatment of Slaves on Lloyd's Plantation,” the first three paragraphs; opens “THE heart-rending incidents, related in the foregoing chapter, led me, thus early, to…”; closes “…to slavery--and one which all the powers of slavery were unable to silence or extinguish.”.

questions.prompt: What answers did the child receive to “Why am I a slave?”, and which troubled him most?
facilitatorNotes: That God made white people masters and Black people slaves, and that God is good and knows best. The second was worse, because Esther’s suffering contradicted any notion of goodness. He also asks how anyone could know God’s intention.
evidence: This was less satisfactory than the first statement
It was not good to let old master cut the flesh off Esther, and make her cry so.

questions.prompt: How does the child test the claim that colour explains slavery?
facilitatorNotes: By counter-examples “on both sides, and in the middle”: free Black people, white people who held no slaves, and nearly white people who were enslaved. One exception in each category is enough to refute the theory.
evidence: Color, therefore, was a very unsatisfactory basis for slavery.

questions.prompt: “It was not color, but crime, not God, but man.” What follows from that conclusion, and why is it knowledge “quite worth possessing” even though it increased his suffering?
facilitatorNotes: If slavery is a human crime, kidnapping enforced by law, then “what man can make, man can unmake.” The knowledge brings hatred and pain without means of escape, but it grounds the dream of freedom he calls “a constant menace to slavery.”
evidence: what man can make, man can unmake
Yet it was knowledge quite worth possessing.

questions.prompt: How reliable is this account of a seven-year-old’s reasoning, written by a man of thirty-seven?
facilitatorNotes: The adult has shaped the child’s thinking into an argument, and “I was master of the subject” sounds compressed and heightened. The questions in the child’s idiom (“Did they go up in the sky and learn it?”) sound authentic. Readers can grant the questions and weigh the speed of the conclusions.
evidence: Did they go up in the sky and learn it?
I was master of the subject.

readings.title: Nelly’s resistance — excerpt
readings.challenge: Test a general lesson against the single story told to support it.
readings.focus: A woman’s resistance to a whipping, and what resistance gains on a plantation.
readings.context: Douglass, still a child on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation, says that after Esther’s whipping he saw many such scenes. Mr. Sevier is the overseer; a sloop is a single-masted boat that carried the plantation’s goods to Baltimore; a “hand” is a worker.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes an overseer’s struggle with a woman and her whipping in front of her children, with a profane threat printed with letters omitted.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Treatment of Slaves on Lloyd's Plantation,” the paragraph on Nelly and the overseers Sevier, Hopkins and Gore; opens “Up to the time of the brutal flogging of my Aunt Esther--for she was my own aunt--and the…”; closes “…that he was no improvement on Mr. Sevier, except that he was less noisy and less profane.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass call “impudence” “one of the commonest and most indefinite” offences?
facilitatorNotes: It can mean anything: the tone of an answer, answering, not answering, a look, a gait. A charge with no fixed content gives the accuser unlimited power.
evidence: This may mean almost anything, or nothing at all
in answering at all; in not answering

questions.prompt: Douglass concedes that “according to all slaveholding standards, here was a genuine instance of impudence.” What is he doing with this phrase?
facilitatorNotes: He uses irony: Nelly is a spirited wife and mother whose self-respect is exactly what slaveholders call impudence. Granting the charge exposes the standard.
evidence: according to all slaveholding standards, here was a genuine instance of impudence

questions.prompt: What general lesson does Douglass draw from Nelly’s resistance, and does her story fully support it?
facilitatorNotes: “He is whipped oftenest, who is whipped easiest”: the resister may become “in the end, a freeman” in spirit. Nelly was severely whipped but not subdued, yet Douglass admits he does not know whether Sevier tried again, and Sevier soon died. The lesson rests partly on other cases, such as the man who told Rigby Hopkins he could shoot but not whip him.
evidence: He is whipped oftenest, who is whipped easiest
I do not know that Mr. Sevier ever undertook to whip Nelly again.

questions.prompt: How does Douglass portray Mr. Sevier, and what does the comparison with the overseers after him suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Sevier is a bull-dog with teeth worn down by tobacco and rage, mourned by no one. Hopkins is “as good as any man can be, and yet be an overseer,” and Gore is no improvement. The office limits even the best man who holds it.
evidence: like a savage bull-dog
as good as any man can be, and yet be an overseer

readings.title: Songs of the great house farm — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what a song’s words say from what its sound testifies to.
readings.focus: Why the singing of enslaved people was not evidence of their happiness.
readings.context: Douglass, about seven or eight, lives on Colonel Edward Lloyd’s great plantation on the Wye River in Maryland. Once a month, people from the outlying farms came to the home or “great house” farm to collect their allowance of food. Douglass quotes his own Narrative of 1845, written ten years before this book. The Pearl was a schooner on which about seventy-seven enslaved people tried to escape from Washington in 1848; they were caught. One full stop, after “chains,” failed to print in some copies of the 1855 printing; it is supplied from a copy that shows it (University of Toronto copy, Internet Archive mybondagemyfreed00douguoft, p. 99).
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Treatment of Slaves on Lloyd's Plantation,” from allowance day to the singing of the slaves; opens “I have already referred to the business-like aspect of Col. Lloyd's plantation. This…”; closes “…and peace. Slaves sing more to make themselves happy, than to express their happiness.”.

questions.prompt: Why was being chosen to go to the great house farm “deemed a high honor,” and what does Douglass think the competitors really wanted?
facilitatorNotes: It was taken as a mark of confidence and a chance to see the grand place and the sailors’ trinkets. But Douglass thinks the “chief motive” was escape from the field’s monotony and the overseer’s lash: on the road a man was “comparatively free” and “had time to think.” The privilege is measured by a few hours unwatched.
evidence: probably, the chief motive of the competitors for the place, was, a desire to break the dull monotony of the field
the slave was comparatively free; and, if thoughtful, he had time to think.

questions.prompt: What practical reasons for singing does Douglass give before he turns to what the songs meant?
facilitatorNotes: Masters and overseers disliked silence (“Make a noise”), and teamsters’ singing told the overseer where they were and that they were working. Singing was partly required and partly a signal, so its sound proves nothing about contentment. Only then does he say the songs “were not always merry because they were wild.”
evidence: A silent slave is not liked by masters or overseers.
it was one means of letting the overseer know where they were

questions.prompt: The quoted song calls the old master “a good old master.” How can a song that flatters the master also be “a testimony against slavery”?
facilitatorNotes: The words were chosen to please the owner and win “a favorable glance,” while the improvised parts were “jargon to others, but full of meaning to themselves.” The testimony lies in the tones, “loud, long and deep,” not in the words. Douglass hears the same wailing in Ireland during the famine, a comparison that ties the songs to grief, not to race.
evidence: My old master is a good old master,
jargon to others, but full of meaning to themselves
Every tone was a testimony against slavery

questions.prompt: “I was myself within the circle, so that I neither saw nor heard as those without might see and hear.” What does this say about when understanding comes, and how does it prepare the paragraph’s last sentence?
facilitatorNotes: Inside the experience the child could not interpret it; understanding came later and from outside. Outsiders, though, made the opposite mistake and took singing for joy. The castaway on an island and the Pearl’s captives singing in chains show that sorrow sings too, so “Slaves sing more to make themselves happy, than to express their happiness.”
evidence: I was myself within the circle, so that I neither saw nor heard as those without might see and hear.
Slaves sing more to make themselves happy, than to express their happiness.

readings.title: The boast of physical comfort — excerpt
readings.challenge: Check a general claim against the figures offered to refute it.
readings.focus: Food, clothing, beds and sleep on Lloyd’s plantation, and the whip that enforced the hours.
readings.context: Douglass, a child on Colonel Edward Lloyd’s plantation in Maryland, has described the monthly “allowance day.” Here he answers the claim, common in defences of slavery, that enslaved Americans lived better than the poor of Europe. Unbolted meal is unsifted, with the bran left in; a peck is a quarter of a bushel; crash is coarse linen used for towels; slazily means flimsily; a cowskin is a heavy whip of dried hide, and a cat-o’-nine-tails a whip of knotted cords.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes children left nearly naked and the whipping of field hands; uses the period phrase “little heathen.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Treatment of Slaves on Lloyd's Plantation,” from the allowance of food and clothing to the cowskin; opens “It is the boast of slaveholders, that their slaves enjoy more of the physical comforts of…”; closes “…With him, it is literally a word and a blow, and, in most cases, the blow comes first.”.

questions.prompt: What claim does Douglass test here, and what kind of evidence does he bring against it?
facilitatorNotes: The slaveholders’ boast that their slaves enjoy more comfort “than the peasantry of any country.” He answers with quantities: eight pounds of pork, a bushel of meal of which fifteen per cent was unfit, a pint of salt, clothing worth no more than eight dollars a year, and he converts the month into “a quarter of a pound of meat per day.” Figures make the claim checkable and keep his tone level.
evidence: My experience contradicts this.
living on a fraction more than a quarter of a pound of meat per day, and less than a peck of corn-meal per week

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass say that time to sleep mattered more than beds?
facilitatorNotes: After the field the enslaved still had to wash, mend and cook for themselves, so their own work ate into the night, and the horn called them out at first light. “The night, however, is shortened at both ends” compresses the whole system into one sentence.
evidence: Time to sleep was of far greater importance
The night, however, is shortened at both ends.

questions.prompt: Douglass describes the cowskin exactly: its material, length, taper and colours. Why give a whip such a careful description?
facilitatorNotes: His readers in the North had seldom seen one, so precision gives credibility. The painted colours make a weapon look like an ornament, which is chilling. He ends by turning a proverb: “a word and a blow” becomes a blow first. The description shows that punishment needs no cause: the temptation “is ever strong.”
evidence: Cowskins are painted red, blue and green, and are the favorite slave whip.
it is literally a word and a blow, and, in most cases, the blow comes first.

questions.prompt: What do the young mothers in the field add to Douglass’s account of the “allowance”?
facilitatorNotes: Time, like food, is rationed: an hour to nurse, or the child left in a fence corner “to prevent loss of time.” The phrase is the system’s own accounting, and it puts a baby’s needs below the overseer’s schedule.
evidence: to leave them in the corner of the fences, to prevent loss of time in nursing them

readings.title: Ash cake, and the turn to the great house — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow the turn from description to a moral argument, and test it against what came before.
readings.focus: A field hand’s day, and Douglass’s claim that slavery harms the master too.
readings.context: Douglass, a child on Colonel Edward Lloyd’s plantation in Maryland, has listed the food and clothing given to the field hands and described the overseer’s whip. Ash cake is cornmeal dough baked in the ashes of a fire; the turning row is the strip at a field’s end where the plough turns. In the sentence about the field hands’ tools, “noes” is the 1855 printing’s misprint for hoes, kept as printed. Viz. means namely.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass calls field hands “human cattle” to condemn how they were treated, and describes an overseer’s blows.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Treatment of Slaves on Lloyd's Plantation,” from the slaves’ meals in the field to the end of the chapter; opens “As a general rule, slaves do not come to the quarters for either breakfast or dinner, but…”; closes “…occasionally, to assist the reader in the proper understanding of the facts narrated.”.

questions.prompt: How does Douglass describe ash cake, and why, by his account, do the enslaved like it?
facilitatorNotes: Ashes coat it “to the depth of a sixteenth part of an inch,” with bran and scales running through; it would “disgust and choke a northern man.” They like it because they are hungry and overworked: they care about quantity, not quality. The liking is evidence of want, not of contentment.
evidence: would disgust and choke a northern man, but it is quite liked by the slaves
more concerned about the quantity than about the quality

questions.prompt: Look at the series “no hope … no sense … no love … no prospect” and the sentence that ends the paragraph. What do they do?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated “no” strips away every motive that drives free labour until only “the dread and terror of the slave-driver’s lash” is left. Then “So goes one day, and so comes and goes another” makes the day endlessly repeatable. The rhythm carries the monotony.
evidence: hurried on by no hope of reward, no sense of gratitude
So goes one day, and so comes and goes another.

questions.prompt: Douglass agrees that “slavery is a greater evil to the master than to the slave.” What difference between the two does he draw, and is the claim convincing after what he has described?
facilitatorNotes: The slave’s miseries are imposed by others; the master’s are self-imposed, so he is “the author of his own subjection.” The harm to the master is moral and spiritual. Some readers find the claim hard to accept beside hunger and the lash; Douglass himself qualifies it (“than many, who utter it, suppose”) and turns to “eternal justice.”
evidence: the slaveholder is a subject, but he is the author of his own subjection
There is more truth in the saying, that slavery is a greater evil to the master than to the slave

questions.prompt: Douglass ends, “let others philosophize; it is my province here to relate and describe.” How well does that describe what he actually does?
facilitatorNotes: He presents himself as a witness who comments only to help the reader understand. Yet he has just philosophized about masters and justice. Readers may see a modest pose, a strategy to keep his testimony credible, or an honest statement of priorities.
evidence: it is my province here to relate and describe

readings.title: The great house and its table — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a lavish catalogue for the words that tell you who paid for it.
readings.focus: The luxury of the Lloyds’ house set against the field, and whether anyone there is happy.
readings.context: Douglass turns from the quarters and fields of Colonel Edward Lloyd’s Maryland plantation to the Lloyds’ mansion, which he saw as a boy from outside. “Purple and fine linen” comes from Jesus’s parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16), in which a rich man feasts while a beggar lies starving at his gate. A desideratum is a thing wanted; phaetons, barouches and sulkeys are carriages; terrapin is a turtle; “Mas’” is master.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass contrasts the complexion and dress of house servants with those of field hands in period terms.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Life in the Great House,” from the opening to the troubles of the Lloyds; opens “THE close-fisted stinginess that fed the poor slave on coarse corn-meal and tainted meat;…”; closes “…wicked, nor to the idler, is there any solid peace: "Troubled, like the restless sea."”.

questions.prompt: The first sentence begins in the field and ends at the great house. How does its structure enact the contrast?
facilitatorNotes: Three “that” clauses pile up the slave’s coarse meal, crashy shirts and the mother nursing in the fence corner, and then all of it “wholly vanishes” at the house. The reader crosses from field to mansion inside one sentence, as the wealth itself is carried from one to the other.
evidence: wholly vanishes on approaching the sacred precincts of the great house

questions.prompt: Douglass lists the foods of the Lloyds’ table at great length. Which words remind the reader where the luxury comes from?
facilitatorNotes: “Blood-bought luxuries,” fields and seas “made tributary,” birds “fat and fatting for the destined vortex,” and the “huge family net”: the language of tribute, consumption and capture. The list impresses, then accuses. Even the smells are rationed: “The odors I shared with the winds.”
evidence: The table groans under the heavy and blood-bought luxuries
are caught in this huge family net
The odors I shared with the winds

questions.prompt: What does the appearance of the house servants, “a sort of black aristocracy,” prove, and what does it hide?
facilitatorNotes: They were chosen for looks and grace and dressed in their owners’ cast-off silks, so a guest saw well-clad, graceful servants and a generous host. Douglass adds that the host was generous only “Viewed from his own table, and not from the field”: the display depends on the field and does not change the servants’ status as property.
evidence: These servants constituted a sort of black aristocracy
Viewed from his own table, and not from the field, the colonel was a model of generous hospitality.

questions.prompt: Paragraph 124 opens with four questions. Whose voice do they imitate, and how does Douglass answer them?
facilitatorNotes: A dazzled visitor’s, or a defender’s (“Who, but a fanatic”). He answers like a preacher: the luxury brings gout and fretfulness, and the slave on his plank sleeps better than the “feverish voluptuary.” Some readers find this consolation too neat after the field; others see it setting up the next pages on the Lloyds’ “restless discontent.”
evidence: Who, but a fanatic, could get up any sympathy
The poor slave, on his hard, pine plank, but scantily covered with his thin blanket, sleeps more soundly than the feverish voluptuary

readings.title: Old Barney and William Wilks — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Douglass saw, what was whispered, and what he infers.
readings.focus: Two men at the Lloyd stables: one humiliated, one probably the colonel’s son.
readings.context: Colonel Edward Lloyd kept about thirty-five horses for pleasure at his Maryland plantation, cared for by two enslaved men, Old Barney and his son. An ostler looks after horses; a farrier shoes and treats them; lampers is a swelling in a horse’s mouth; to bleed was a common treatment. Amalgamation was the period word for sexual relations and children between white and Black people. Austin Woldfolk was a well-known slave trader in Baltimore.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. An old man is made to kneel and is whipped; the passage concerns a slaveholder’s son by an enslaved woman and his sale.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Life in the Great House,” from the stables and Old Barney to William Wilks; opens “I had excellent opportunities of witnessing the restless discontent and the capricious…”; closes “…Practical amalgamation is common in every neighborhood where I have been in slavery.”.

questions.prompt: What complaints were made about the horses, and what was Barney not allowed to do in reply?
facilitatorNotes: Dust in the hair, a twist in the reins, a mane not lying straight: trifles, so that “something was always wrong.” Barney had to stand “hat in hand, lips sealed.” Douglass imagines a free ostler’s answer, “your remedy is to dismiss me,” which shows what the enslaved man could not say.
evidence: something was always wrong
Barney must stand, hat in hand, lips sealed, never answering a word
your remedy is to dismiss me

questions.prompt: Douglass doubts the light riding whip did Barney much bodily harm. Why, then, does he call the scene one of the most humiliating he ever saw?
facilitatorNotes: The harm is degradation: two old men, “equals at the bar of God,” one kneeling bare-shouldered on damp ground before the other, “a worm of the dust.” He also says it was the only time he saw a slave made to kneel for a whipping, an exception that makes his testimony more credible.
evidence: equals at the bar of God
humbly kneeling before a worm of the dust
this was the first and the last time I ever saw Old Barney, or any other slave, compelled to kneel to receive a whipping

questions.prompt: What evidence does Douglass offer that William Wilks was Colonel Lloyd’s son? How strong is it, and how carefully does he state his conclusion?
facilitatorNotes: The resemblance to Murray Lloyd, William’s unusual freedom, Murray’s hatred, a whipping followed by a gold watch, and his mysterious self-purchase. Douglass reports a whisper, asks “Is there not room to suspect,” and concludes only that nothing forbids “the supposition.” The evidence is circumstantial, and he presents it as such.
evidence: It was whispered, and pretty generally admitted as a fact
Is there not room to suspect
to forbid the supposition that William Wilks was the son of Edward Lloyd

questions.prompt: Why does the colonel’s whipping of William fail, by Douglass’s account, and what does the gold watch reveal about his position?
facilitatorNotes: The whipping was meant to calm Murray, but “It was a compromise, and defeated itself”: the colonel at once “atoned” with a gift. Owner and father pull against each other; the watch apologises for a beating the owner had the power to give. Selling William ends the conflict at William’s cost.
evidence: It was a compromise, and defeated itself
atoned to William for the abuse, by giving him a gold watch and chain

readings.title: “Who do you belong to?” — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a short anecdote as the evidence for a general rule.
readings.focus: Why enslaved people told strangers that their masters were kind, and what their quarrels about masters reveal.
readings.context: Douglass is ending his account of Colonel Edward Lloyd’s plantation in Maryland. Lloyd owned so many people that he did not know them all by sight. A “Georgia trader” bought enslaved people in Maryland to sell in the cotton states of the Deep South; being sold south, away from family, was among the most feared punishments. Jacob Jepson was a neighbouring slaveholder. The 1855 page misprints “addresssed,” kept as printed.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A man is chained and sold away from his family for answering a question honestly.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Life in the Great House,” the last paragraph; opens “Col. Lloyd was not in the way of knowing much of the real opinions and feelings of his…”; closes “…thought to be bad enough; but to be a poor man's slave, was deemed a disgrace, indeed.”.

questions.prompt: Reread the conversation on the road. What does the man actually say, and why does Douglass call it “the simple truth”?
facilitatorNotes: He is treated badly, worked too hard, and fed enough “such as it is.” The answers are exact and restrained, not abusive. He does not know he is speaking to his owner, and he is sold “without a moment’s warning” weeks later. The punishment falls on plain answers to plain questions.
evidence: Yes, sir, he gives me enough, such as it is.
This is the penalty of telling the simple truth, in answer to a series of plain questions.

questions.prompt: How does the story explain the maxim “a still tongue makes a wise head,” and what does Douglass mean by saying that, in keeping silent, the enslaved “prove themselves a part of the human family”?
facilitatorNotes: With spies and sales as the cost of honesty, silence is reasonable self-protection, the choice any people would make. So the contentment slaves report to strangers is no evidence of contentment; it is evidence of fear, which marks them as human, not as uniquely docile.
evidence: a still tongue makes a wise head
they prove themselves a part of the human family

questions.prompt: Douglass admits he always said he had a kind master, yet denies he was lying. How does he justify this?
facilitatorNotes: He judged kindness “by the standard of kindness set up by slaveholders around us”: compared with others, his master might be called kind. The word changes meaning inside slavery. Readers can debate whether a relative truth is an honest one.
evidence: I always measured the kindness of my master by the standard of kindness set up by slaveholders around us

questions.prompt: What explains, by Douglass’s account, the fights between Lloyd’s slaves and Jepson’s slaves? Is he sympathetic or critical?
facilitatorNotes: Each side borrowed the master’s greatness: riches against the power to “whip Col. Lloyd.” Douglass calls it a prejudice that “slaves are like other people” share, and ends that being “a poor man’s slave” was a disgrace. He is gently satirical but understanding: people claim dignity where they can, even through their owners.
evidence: They seemed to think that the greatness of their masters was transferable to themselves.
to be a poor man's slave, was deemed a disgrace, indeed.

readings.title: Austin Gore and the murder of Denby — excerpt
readings.challenge: Weigh a character sketch, an eyewitness account and the killer’s defence against one another.
readings.focus: An overseer who killed from a sense of duty, and a system that accepted his reasons.
readings.context: On Colonel Edward Lloyd’s Maryland plantation, the brutal overseer Mr. Sevier had died and been followed by the milder Mr. Hopkins. Douglass now introduces Hopkins’s successor. The fish-women of Paris and coal-heavers of London were rough working trades; “take the place” means seize the plantation; a nine days’ wonder is a sensation soon forgotten. Douglass gives the murdered man’s name as Denby or Demby.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Narrates an overseer shooting a young enslaved man dead in a creek, with his blood described, and the killer’s impunity.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “A Chapter of Horrors,” from the new overseer to Gore’s defence; opens “As I have already intimated elsewhere, the slaves on Col. Lloyd's plantation, whose hard…”; closes “…go further in a court of law, than the united testimony of ten thousand black witnesses.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass treats overseers as a class but says Gore was “something more.” How does he distinguish Gore from the others, and why is that more frightening?
facilitatorNotes: Gore had no swagger or jokes; he was grave, self-possessed and had “something of the lawful master.” He whipped “from a sense of duty, and feared no consequences.” Cruelty from conviction is steadier than cruelty from temper, which is why Douglass compares him to a pirate chief.
evidence: He was an overseer; but he was something more.
When he whipped, he seemed to do so from a sense of duty, and feared no consequences.

questions.prompt: Why might Douglass include the admission “I write from sound, and the sounds on Lloyd’s plantation are not very certain” in his account of a murder?
facilitatorNotes: He is honest about what he cannot know, the exact spelling of a name no record kept, while insisting on what he does know: “I knew him well.” The admission marks how little the enslaved were recorded and strengthens the credibility of his main claims.
evidence: I write from sound, and the sounds on Lloyd's plantation are not very certain.
I knew him well.

questions.prompt: Follow Gore’s defence step by step. What does each step assume, and how does Douglass answer it?
facilitatorNotes: Necessity, an “unmanageable” man, a dangerous example, and then the slide to “the freedom of the slaves, and the enslavement of the whites.” Each step treats any refusal as rebellion. Douglass calls the argument a “cowardly alarm-cry” used to excuse a thousand crimes, and notes that the murder never reached a court.
evidence: that cowardly alarm-cry
the freedom of the slaves, and the enslavement of the whites

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass close with the rule that the enslaved witnesses “could neither institute a suit, nor testify against the murderer”?
facilitatorNotes: The killing happened in front of many people, yet in law there were no witnesses. The comparison, Gore’s word against “ten thousand black witnesses,” shows that the law itself guaranteed impunity. The crime is personal; the cover is legal.
evidence: His bare word would go further in a court of law, than the united testimony of ten thousand black witnesses.

readings.title: Murders that went unpunished — excerpt
readings.challenge: Track how Douglass builds a general claim about law from a series of cases.
readings.focus: Why laws that nominally protected enslaved people could not be enforced.
readings.context: Recap: Austin Gore, the overseer, shot Denby, a young enslaved man who stood in a creek and refused to come out to be whipped; Colonel Lloyd accepted Gore’s defence and kept him on. Talbot County and St. Michael’s are on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. A coroner’s jury inquires into a sudden death; condign means deserved; a musket is a long gun.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes several killings and a shooting, including the beating to death of a teenage girl; two sayings Douglass reports use a racial slur.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “A Chapter of Horrors,” from Gore’s peace with Colonel Lloyd to the end of the chapter; opens “All that Mr. Gore had to do, was to make his peace with Col. Lloyd. This done, and the…”; closes “…of my early childhood, and will relieve the kind reader of these heart-sickening details.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass expects his account to be called “false and malicious.” How does he answer that charge in these paragraphs?
facilitatorNotes: He names people and places (St. Michael’s, Talbot County, Thomas Lanman, Mrs. Hicks, Beal Bondley), mentions a coroner’s jury and a warrant, and reports a killer’s public boasting. “I speak advisedly” claims careful knowledge. He also refuses to argue further: “believe it or not.”
evidence: I can only say--believe it or not--that I have said nothing but the literal truth, gainsay it who may.
I speak advisedly when I say this

questions.prompt: In the Hicks case a coroner’s jury met and a warrant was issued. Why does Douglass still say the community failed?
facilitatorNotes: The jury named the cause of death and the warrant existed, but it “was never served.” Douglass blames a moral sense “blunted” by how ordinary such horrors were. The forms of justice existed without its substance.
evidence: the moral sense of the community was blunted too entirely by the ordinary nature of slavery horrors
that warrant was never served

questions.prompt: What does Douglass conclude about laws “for the protection of the lives of the slaves,” and why must they fail?
facilitatorNotes: Those the laws protect may not testify against the only people likely to harm them, so the laws cannot be enforced; he never knew a slaveholder hanged or imprisoned for killing a slave. The argument returns to the evidence rule that ended the Denby story, now as a general law.
evidence: are not permitted to give evidence, in courts of law, against the only class of persons from whom abuse, outrage and murder might be reasonably apprehended

questions.prompt: The chapter ends, “and will relieve the kind reader of these heart-sickening details.” Why might Douglass address the reader this way here?
facilitatorNotes: It acknowledges what the reader can bear and keeps sympathetic readers with him. It may also be pointed: the reader can be relieved by turning a page, as the people in these stories could not. Both readings fit the chapter’s restraint.
evidence: will relieve the kind reader of these heart-sickening details

readings.title: Miss Lucretia’s bread — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how an adult measures a child’s suffering against what he saw others suffer.
readings.focus: Small kindnesses, hunger and cold in a child’s life on the plantation.
readings.context: Douglass, about eight, lives in the house of his owner, Captain Aaron Anthony, who manages Colonel Lloyd’s farms in Maryland. Aunt Katy, an enslaved woman, runs the kitchen; Lucretia Auld, the captain’s daughter, is married to Thomas Auld. Mas’ Daniel is a young Lloyd who protected him. Balsam is a healing ointment; a termagant is a quarrelsome woman; mush is boiled cornmeal; “eat” was an accepted past tense.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Aunt Katy’s insult, as Douglass reports it, contains a racial slur; describes hunger, cold, a head wound and children fed from a trough.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Personal Treatment of the Author,” from the opening through the children’s meals; opens “I HAVE nothing cruel or shocking to relate of my own personal experience, while I…”; closes “…her anything unfavorable of me, she always believed the worst, and was sure to whip me.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass begins, “I HAVE nothing cruel or shocking to relate of my own personal experience.” How does the rest of the passage complicate that statement?
facilitatorNotes: He goes on to a gashed forehead, hunger, near nakedness in winter, a meal sack for a bed and feet cracked by frost. He means he was not whipped severely; measured against the murders and floggings he has described, his own suffering seems small to him. The reader may judge otherwise.
evidence: is all that I can mention of this sort
I was kept almost in a state of nudity

questions.prompt: What does Miss Lucretia actually do for Douglass, and why does he value it so much?
facilitatorNotes: She binds his wound with her own balsam and gives him bread when he sings under her window. He admits her interest “was never very marked,” but in a cold household “the slightest word or look of kindness passed … for its full value.” Singing for bread links back to his argument that singing could be a petition, not joy.
evidence: the slightest word or look of kindness passed, with me, for its full value
a habit of singing, which the good lady very soon came to understand as a petition for a piece of bread

questions.prompt: How does Douglass make the children’s meal degrading, and what rule decided who ate?
facilitatorNotes: Mush in a trough set on the floor or the ground; the children “called, like so many pigs,” eating with oyster shells and shingles, “none with spoons.” Speed and strength decided everything, and Aunt Katy’s dislike made him “the most unlucky.” The comparison to pigs is his, aimed at the treatment, not the children.
evidence: the children were called, like so many pigs; and like so many pigs they would come
He that eat fastest got most, and he that was strongest got the best place

questions.prompt: “My feet have been so cracked with the frost, that the pen with which I am writing might be laid in the gashes.” What does this sentence do that a plain statement of cold would not?
facilitatorNotes: It joins the child’s body to the adult author: the pen that writes the book measures the wound. Writing becomes testimony from the body, and the image fixes the scale of the cracks. Some readers also hear a reminder that the boy who slept in a meal sack now writes books.
evidence: My feet have been so cracked with the frost, that the pen with which I am writing might be laid in the gashes.

readings.title: Leaving the plantation — excerpt
readings.challenge: Weigh a child’s certainties as an adult reports them.
readings.focus: A child who knows slavery is wrong, and a departure that costs him nothing.
readings.context: Douglass, about nine, has described hunger, cold and the small kindnesses of Miss Lucretia, his owner’s daughter, on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation in Maryland. Now he learns he will be sent to Baltimore to live with Hugh Auld, brother of Lucretia’s husband. Scurf is flaky dead skin; mange is a skin disease of animals; the Sally Lloyd was the plantation’s sloop.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A child wishes he had never been born.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Personal Treatment of the Author,” from his childhood despair to cousin Tom’s Baltimore; opens “As I grew older and more thoughtful, I was more and more filled with a sense of my…”; closes “…curiosity very much; and, indeed, which heightened my hopes of happiness in my new home.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass says that at nine he knew slavery was a crime “Without any appeal to books, to laws, or to authorities.” On what does he base that knowledge, and do you find the claim believable?
facilitatorNotes: On a single premise: “it was enough to accept God as a father.” He also argues that children sometimes reach in a moment “conclusions which no subsequent experience can shake.” Readers may accept the moral clarity of a child, or suspect the adult author of sharpening the memory; both are reasonable.
evidence: it was enough to accept God as a father, to regard slavery as a crime
reach, in a moment, conclusions which no subsequent experience can shake

questions.prompt: The boy envies the black-birds, “in whose wild and sweet songs I fancied them so happy!” How does this moment connect with Douglass’s argument about the songs of the enslaved?
facilitatorNotes: Here the child makes the outsider’s mistake: he hears song and assumes joy (“fancied”). Douglass has argued that outsiders made the same error about slaves’ singing. The moment shows how natural the error is.
evidence: in whose wild and sweet songs I fancied them so happy

questions.prompt: Why does leaving cost Douglass so little? What does his list of family members show?
facilitatorNotes: His mother is dead, his grandmother far away, Aunt Katy is a tormentor and his brothers and sisters are “comparatively, strangers.” The plantation “was not home, but a prison.” The absence of grief is itself evidence of “the family-destroying power of slavery.”
evidence: it was not home, but a prison to me
the family-destroying power of slavery

questions.prompt: How does Douglass make cousin Tom both comic and important?
facilitatorNotes: Tom stutters yet gives an “eloquent description,” and insists that even the great house “was nothing to Baltimore.” His trumpet and stories of steamboats are funny boasts, but they give the boy a destination to hope for, and Douglass scrubs himself, “working for the first time in the hope of reward.”
evidence: though not fluent (he stuttered immoderately,) in speech, he had inspired me
working for the first time in the hope of reward

readings.title: To Baltimore — excerpt
readings.challenge: Hold a child’s first impressions and an adult’s judgment of them side by side.
readings.focus: A voyage, a welcome, and Douglass’s reading of his removal as providence.
readings.context: In 1826 Douglass, not yet ten, sails on Colonel Lloyd’s sloop down the Miles River and up Chesapeake Bay to Baltimore, a busy port. Annapolis is Maryland’s capital; Fell’s Point is Baltimore’s shipbuilding district. Hugh and Sophia Auld are his new master and mistress. The lines he quotes adapt Hamlet’s “There’s a divinity that shapes our ends, / Rough-hew them how we will.”
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Personal Treatment of the Author,” from the voyage to the end of the chapter; opens “We sailed out of Miles river for Baltimore early on a Saturday morning. I remember only…”; closes “…of my lot. This good spirit was from God; and to him I offer thanksgiving and praise.”.

questions.prompt: On setting sail, Douglass looks back once and then goes to the bow. What does his movement on the boat suggest?
facilitatorNotes: A deliberate last look at the plantation, then attention to “what was in the distance, rather than what was near by or behind.” The physical move from stern to bow becomes a turn from past to future; the open bay looks like “a shoreless ocean.”
evidence: gave to Col. Lloyd's plantation what I hoped would be the last look I should ever give to it
interesting myself in what was in the distance, rather than what was near by or behind

questions.prompt: Annapolis was “inferior to many a factory village in New England,” yet the boy felt like a traveller seeing Rome. What does this double view achieve?
facilitatorNotes: The adult knows better and says so, but he honours the child’s wonder rather than mocking it. The comparison is gently funny and shows how small the boy’s world had been: the state house dome outdoes the great house.
evidence: inferior to many a factory village in New England
a pitch very little below that reached by travelers at the first view of Rome

questions.prompt: How is Douglass received in Baltimore, and what does the detail that old master gave him to “little Tommy” reveal beneath the kindness?
facilitatorNotes: Sophia Auld’s face is “lighted with the kindliest emotions,” and the boy loves Tommy at once. But he is a present to a child, expected to become Tommy’s “legal property.” The warmth exists inside ownership, and “not a cloud above the horizon” may be ironic, since readers sense clouds to come.
evidence: that old master made a present of me
with not a cloud above the horizon

questions.prompt: Douglass calls his removal the work of a “Divinity that shapes our ends.” How does he present this belief, and how does he defend it?
facilitatorNotes: He weighs chance (“the light of human likelihoods”) and admits he may be called “superstitious and egotistical,” but says hiding the belief would be false to his history. He links it to a lifelong conviction that slavery would not hold him. Readers can weigh providence, chance and Douglass’s own choices.
evidence: I may be deemed superstitious and egotistical
something more intelligent than chance, and something more certain than luck

readings.title: Mrs. Hamilton’s slaves — excerpt
readings.challenge: Test a general observation against the exception Douglass sets beside it.
readings.focus: How a city restrained some cruelty, and who is answerable for what it allowed.
readings.context: Douglass, about ten, has been sent from Colonel Lloyd’s plantation to Baltimore, to the household of Hugh and Sophia Auld, where his mistress at first treats him kindly. Here he compares slavery in the city with what he saw on the plantation. Odium is public hatred; excoriated means with the skin torn off; a cowskin is a heavy whip of dried hide; offal is waste meat thrown out. The “drinking system” echoes the temperance movement of the 1850s, which blamed the trade in alcohol for drunkenness.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes the beating and starving of two teenage girls in detail; their mistress’s insult, as Douglass reports it, is a racial slur.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “Life in Baltimore,” from city slavery to the end of the chapter; opens “I had resided but a short time in Baltimore, before I observed a marked difference in the…”; closes “…on those who, by precept and example, or by indifference, uphold the drinking system.”.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Douglass, are city slaves treated better than plantation slaves? What does the rule he quotes, “Work them, flog them, if need be, but don’t starve them,” show about the limits of that improvement?
facilitatorNotes: A dense population of non-slaveholders brings a “general sense of decency,” and few masters want the “odium” of cruelty. But the maxim shows how low the standard is: flogging is accepted, and only starving is shameful. The city restrains the visible excess, not the system.
evidence: Slavery dislikes a dense population, in which there is a majority of non-slaveholders.
Work them, flog them, if need be, but don't starve them.

questions.prompt: Douglass repeatedly sets Mrs. Hamilton’s religion beside her cruelty. Find the phrases that do this. What is the effect of the final image of her “singing her sweet hymns”?
facilitatorNotes: “Church going and Christian city,” “seeming piety,” “psalm-singing Mrs. Hamilton.” The last sentence is bitter irony: the whip and the hymn alternate in one breath, as if her soul “were sighing for the holy realms of paradise.” Douglass attacks religion used as a cover for cruelty, not religion itself, a distinction he draws elsewhere in the book.
evidence: in the refined, church going and Christian city of Baltimore
Then the lady would go on, singing her sweet hymns, as though her righteous soul were sighing for the holy realms of paradise.

questions.prompt: “I have frequently felt her head.” Why might Douglass include this detail and the nickname the street boys gave Mary?
facilitatorNotes: Touching the sores makes him a witness by hand as well as by eye, which answers doubting readers. The nickname shows that the whole street could see the injuries and turned them into a joke: the cruelty was public knowledge, not a hidden secret.
evidence: I have frequently felt her head, and found it nearly covered over with festering sores
the boys in the street knew her only by the name of

questions.prompt: The neighbours condemned Mrs. Hamilton. Why does Douglass still hold the “upholders of the slave system” responsible, and how does his comparison with the “drinking system” make the point?
facilitatorNotes: The same people who censured her would have punished anyone who interfered with her “right” to beat her slaves; disapproval without protection changes nothing. As temperance reformers blamed those who upheld the trade in drink, not only the drunkard, Douglass blames those who uphold slavery, including by “indifference.”
evidence: would have condemned and promptly punished any attempt to interfere with Mrs. Hamilton's right
as drunkenness is chargeable on those who, by precept and example, or by indifference, uphold the drinking system

readings.title: How a mistress is made — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that cruelty is learned, using one person as the evidence.
readings.focus: Sophia Auld’s change from a kind teacher to an enemy of his reading.
readings.context: Douglass, about ten, lives in Baltimore with Hugh and Sophia Auld and their small son Tommy. Sophia Auld began teaching him the alphabet until her husband forbade it, saying that learning would make a slave unfit to be a slave. Almanacs, printed yearly, forecast the weather; a chattel is a piece of movable property; to set one’s face as a flint is to be immovably determined.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “A Change Came O’er the Spirit of My Dream,” from the opening to his mistress’s fury at his reading; opens “I LIVED in the family of Master Hugh, at Baltimore, seven years, during which time--as…”; closes “…a traitor might be supposed to feel on being discovered in a plot by some dangerous spy.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass says that “Nature has done almost nothing to prepare men and women to be either slaves or slaveholders.” What follows from this claim, and how does Mrs. Auld serve as his evidence?
facilitatorNotes: If neither role is natural, both must be produced by “rigid training, long persisted in.” Mrs. Auld, kind and new to owning a person, had to be trained and hardened before she could forget his human nature. Her change shows slaveholding as something learned, and so something that could have been refused.
evidence: Nothing but rigid training, long persisted in, can perfect the character of the one or the other.
It was, at least, necessary for her to have some training, and some hardening

questions.prompt: Look at the series “I could talk and sing; I could laugh and weep; I could reason and remember; I could love and hate.” What is the list proving, and why is it built in pairs?
facilitatorNotes: Each pair joins capacities a chattel cannot have, expression, feeling, mind and passion, until the conclusion “I was human” follows. The pairs make the list rhythmic and complete, covering the whole person. She “knew and felt” it, so her later treatment required her to suppress what she knew.
evidence: sustained to her only the relation of a chattel
I was human, and she, dear lady, knew and felt me to be so.

questions.prompt: “It may be broken toward the slave, on Sunday, and toward the master on Monday.” What does Douglass mean about conscience, and how does it explain the unhappiness of the whole household?
facilitatorNotes: Conscience cannot be broken in one direction only: once she silenced it toward Douglass, it would fail elsewhere too, so “It must stand entire, or it does not stand at all.” The husband who forced the change was injured in “his domestic peace by the fall,” and the happy home Douglass entered is lost.
evidence: It must stand entire, or it does not stand at all.
He, not less than the other parties, was injured in his domestic peace by the fall.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Douglass, did Mrs. Auld become even more opposed to his reading than her husband? In the final simile, who is cast as the traitor?
facilitatorNotes: Having stopped teaching, “she must begin to justify herself to herself,” and the justification hardened her; she “seemed resolved to better his instruction,” perhaps an echo of Shylock in The Merchant of Venice. In the simile she is like a traitor discovered by a spy: her fury suggests guilt, as if the boy reading had found her out.
evidence: she must begin to justify herself to herself
with something of the wrath and consternation which a traitor might be supposed to feel on being discovered in a plot by some dangerous spy

readings.title: Speeches for liberty — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Douglass learned from books from what he says he already knew.
readings.focus: The speeches that gave a boy words for his thoughts, and the distinction between slavery and its incidents.
readings.context: Douglass, about thirteen, has learned to read in secret in Baltimore and has bought, for fifty cents, The Columbian Orator, a popular schoolbook of speeches and dialogues. In one dialogue an enslaved man argues so well that his master frees him. The speakers named were British statesmen: Richard Brinsley Sheridan argued in Parliament for Catholic Emancipation, the removal of legal penalties on Roman Catholics; Lord Chatham, William Pitt and Charles James Fox spoke on the American war and other questions of liberty. In the Bible (Numbers 22) the prophet Balaam beats his donkey for stopping on the road, not seeing the angel that blocks the way.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “A Change Came O’er the Spirit of My Dream,” the last two paragraphs; opens “This, however, was not all the fanaticism which I found in this Columbian Orator. I met…”; closes “…to slavery, just as she herself would have acted, in a reverse of circumstances.”.

questions.prompt: What doubt did the speeches settle, and what did Douglass conclude was the “true foundation” of slavery? Why could a British speech about Catholics do this for an enslaved boy in Baltimore?
facilitatorNotes: He no longer wavered at the idea that God ordained slavery: its foundation was “the pride, the power and the avarice of man.” Sheridan’s case was about other people, but its principle, a “vindication of the rights of man,” applied anywhere. The speeches also gave him words for thoughts that had “died away for want of utterance.”
evidence: had ascertained their true foundation to be in the pride, the power and the avarice of man
enabled me to give tongue to many interesting thoughts, which had frequently flashed through my soul, and died away for want of utterance

questions.prompt: Douglass “almost lost my patience” with religious colored people who believed God required them to submit. Is his impatience fair? Use the next paragraph in your answer.
facilitatorNotes: He calls it “nonsense” and weakness, which can sound harsh. But in the next paragraph he explains where the belief comes from: slaveholders “would have gladly made me believe” they acted under God’s authority. The delusion is taught, so his anger at it also falls on the teachers. Readers may still find the word “weak” unkind to people with no access to his books.
evidence: I could entertain no such nonsense as this
slaveholders would have gladly made me believe that they were merely acting under the authority of God

questions.prompt: Explain Douglass’s comparison of his mistress to Balaam. Who corresponds to the ass and to the angel, and what does the comparison say about her?
facilitatorNotes: She beats him as Balaam beat his donkey, angry at a resistance whose cause she cannot see. The “angel” is what blocks the way, his new knowledge and longing for liberty, which he could not explain to her. The comparison blames her blindness more than her malice, and ends in “Nature had made us friends; slavery made us enemies.”
evidence: Her abuse of me fell upon me like the blows of the false prophet upon his ass
Nature had made us friends; slavery made us enemies.

questions.prompt: “It was slavery--not its mere incidents--that I hated.” Why does Douglass insist on this distinction, and how does the last sentence apply it to his mistress?
facilitatorNotes: Good food and clothing “could not atone for taking my liberty”: no kindness makes ownership acceptable, which answers the claim that well-treated slaves are content. He applies the same principle to her: both are “victims to the same overshadowing evil,” and he trusts that she, in his place, would have acted as he did. The argument rests on the system, not on personal grievances.
evidence: The feeding and clothing me well, could not atone for taking my liberty from me.
just as she herself would have acted, in a reverse of circumstances

readings.title: A word that meant hope — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow how a boy works out the meaning of a word from the anger of the people who use it.
readings.focus: Reading an enemy’s fear as evidence, and a newspaper that teaches what the dictionary will not.
