readings.context: Douglass, about thirteen, lives in Baltimore with Hugh and Sophia Auld; he has taught himself to read in secret, and what he has read has made him wish at times that he had never been born. The abolitionists campaigned to end slavery. Nat Turner led a bloody revolt of enslaved people in Virginia in 1831; cholera, a deadly epidemic disease, reached American cities in 1832. “Allluding” is a misprint in the 1855 printing and stands as printed.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass mentions thoughts of suicide and slaves killing their masters.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Religious Nature Awakened,” the first paragraph; opens “WHILST in the painful state of mind described in the foregoing chapter, almost regretting…”; closes “…the abolition movement, when I saw it supported by the Almighty, and armed with DEATH!”.

questions.prompt: What did the dictionary tell Douglass about “abolition,” and what did it leave out? Where did he find the missing piece?
facilitatorNotes: It gave only “act of abolishing,” leaving him ignorant of the thing to be abolished. The Baltimore American, a slaveholding city’s own newspaper, reported petitions to Congress against slavery in the District of Columbia and the slave trade between the states. The “incendiary information” comes from the slaveholders’ side, which is part of the irony.
evidence: but it left me in ignorance at the very point where I most wanted information
gave me the incendiary information denied me by the dictionary

questions.prompt: How does Douglass reason from what slaveholders said about abolitionists to the conclusion that abolition “could not be unfriendly to the slave”? Is the reasoning sound?
facilitatorNotes: Every escape or act of resistance was blamed on abolition, so whatever it was, it must be on the slave’s side. It is an inference from the enemy’s accusations, and he hedges it (“whatever else it might be”). Readers may call it shrewd rather than certain: it tells him whose side abolition was on, not what it was.
evidence: it was certain to be said, that such a crime was the legitimate fruits of the abolition movement
could not be unfriendly to the slave, nor very friendly to the slaveholder

questions.prompt: Douglass hears “fear, as well as rage” when slaveholders speak of abolitionists. Why does the fear matter more to him than the rage?
facilitatorNotes: Rage shows hostility; fear shows that the abolitionists had power and might succeed. He even says he believed in the movement partly because it alarmed slaveholders’ consciences, so his confidence rests on their unease.
evidence: I saw that there was fear, as well as rage, in the manner of speaking of the abolitionists
I believed in it, partly, because I saw that it alarmed the consciences of slaveholders

questions.prompt: The paragraph ends with abolition “supported by the Almighty, and armed with DEATH!” What does Douglass mean, and why are HOPE and DEATH printed in capitals?
facilitatorNotes: The revolt and the cholera seemed signs that God was angry at slaveholding and was judging the land, so a boy could imagine abolition backed by divine punishment. The capitals mark the two words that carried his feeling: hope for himself, death for the system. Discuss whether the adult narrator endorses the boy’s view or simply reports how it felt; he does not disown it.
evidence: There was HOPE in those words.
when I saw it supported by the Almighty, and armed with DEATH!

readings.title: Father Lawson — excerpt
readings.challenge: Take an old man’s simple faith seriously while noticing what the narrator says it did for him.
readings.focus: Conversion, a spiritual father, and the first prophecy of Douglass’s public work.
readings.context: Douglass, about thirteen, is enslaved in Baltimore by Hugh and Sophia Auld. In the Methodist church a “class” was a small group of members meeting weekly under a lay leader, and a professor of religion was a professing church member. A dray is a heavy cart; a rope-walk is a long shed where rope is made. “The letter” and “the spirit” echo Paul (2 Corinthians 3:6): “the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.”
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Religious Nature Awakened,” from his religious awakening to Uncle Lawson’s promise; opens “Previous to my contemplation of the anti-slavery movement, and its probable results, my…”; closes “…that God would, of His great mercy, and in His own good time, deliver me from my bondage.”.

questions.prompt: Who awakened Douglass’s religious feeling, and what did the preacher teach that might have struck an enslaved boy?
facilitatorNotes: A white Methodist minister, Hanson, preached that all, “bond and free,” were sinners before God, a message that put master and slave on the same footing; Charles Johnson, a colored man, taught him to pray. The weeks of being a “broken-hearted mourner” were the usual path to conversion.
evidence: He thought that all men, great and small, bond and free, were sinners in the sight of God
I was, for weeks, a poor, broken-hearted mourner

questions.prompt: Douglass could teach Lawson “the letter,” and Lawson could teach him “the spirit.” What did each give the other?
facilitatorNotes: The boy was the better reader and helped with hard words; the old man gave understanding and faith. Roles are reversed from what one might expect: in literacy the boy teaches, in wisdom the old man does. Douglass calls him “my spiritual father.”
evidence: for I was a better reader than he
He was my spiritual father

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass name the Rev. Beverly Waugh, “now one of the bishops,” and say he is “careful to state these facts”?
facilitatorNotes: To show the precise influences on him, and that the respectable church reached into a slaveholding household: his mistress belonged to a class led by a future bishop. Naming a public figure also makes the account checkable. Some readers will see a quiet point: Waugh visited, but Lawson was the real teacher.
evidence: now one of the bishops of the Methodist Episcopal church
I am careful to state these facts, that the reader may be able to form an idea of the precise influences

questions.prompt: Uncle Lawson tells him that “the Lord had a great work for me to do.” How does Douglass judge the influence of this, and how did it come true?
facilitatorNotes: Lawson “threw my thoughts into a channel” they never left and fanned his love of knowledge. Douglass did not become a preacher, but he became a public speaker and author against slavery, and the book itself is that work. The promise of freedom “in faith” is honoured, though readers may notice that Douglass will later rely on his own effort as well as prayer.
evidence: He threw my thoughts into a channel from which they have never entirely diverged.
ask the Lord for it, in faith, AND HE WILL GIVE IT TO YOU.

readings.title: The valuation and the division — excerpt
readings.challenge: Hold a personal story and a general argument together: what happened to one boy, and what it shows about the law.
readings.focus: An estate settled by ranking people with livestock, and why removal meant something different to the enslaved.
readings.context: Douglass, about ten, has lived for some years in Baltimore with Hugh and Sophia Auld and their son Tommy, but his legal owner is Captain Anthony, his “old master,” on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. Anthony’s daughter Lucretia is married to Captain Thomas Auld, Hugh’s brother. When a man died intestate (without a will), appraisers valued his property and it was divided among the heirs. A sot is a drunkard; a public out-cry is an auction. “Equaily” is a misprint in the 1855 printing.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes a brutal assault on Douglass’s brother Perry and the threat of sale to the far south.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, “The Vicissitudes of Slave Life,” from the opening to his return to Baltimore; opens “I MUST now ask the reader to go with me a little back in point of time, in my humble…”; closes “…Baltimore, before the matter was decided; and the time really seemed full six months.”.

questions.prompt: At the valuation, Douglass says, people were “leveled at a blow with horses, sheep, horned cattle and swine.” How does the writing in that paragraph make the reader feel the leveling?
facilitatorNotes: He pairs each animal with a kind of person (“Horses and men--cattle and women--pigs and children”), joined by dashes like entries in an inventory, then names the principle in short exclamations: personality “swallowed up” in property. The list forces readers to see as the appraisers saw, which is the horror.
evidence: leveled at a blow with horses, sheep, horned cattle and swine!
Manhood lost in chattelhood!

questions.prompt: Why, according to Douglass, are enslaved people more attached to their home places than free people? What comparison does he use?
facilitatorNotes: Free people move by choice, hope to rise, can write and reunite; young freemen going west feel enthusiasm. For the slave, removal comes as a threat or punishment, with no letters and no reunion, “like a living man going into the tomb.” He is correcting a northern assumption that slaves feel nothing on being sold.
evidence: the slave is a fixture; he has no choice, no goal, no destination
like a living man going into the tomb

questions.prompt: Douglass says he “probably suffered more than most” of the others. Why? Does his reason make their suffering less?
facilitatorNotes: He had known tender treatment; their backs were “callous” from the overseer’s lash, his still “tender.” The metaphor of the overseer writing on “living parchment” makes their callousness an injury, not an advantage: they had been hardened. His point is about fear and loss, not a ranking of pain.
evidence: The overseer had written his character on the living parchment of most of their backs, and left them callous
I had known what it was to experience kind, and even tender treatment

questions.prompt: What does the attack on Perry show about Master Andrew, and why might Douglass credit the outcome to “a kind Providence”?
facilitatorNotes: Andrew stamped on a boy’s head for going to play and threatened Douglass with the same. The outcome depended entirely on the division; no enslaved person had a voice. “A kind Providence” can be read as sincere thanks or as a measure of how much depended on luck; the chapter’s argument supports both.
evidence: seized my brother Perry by the throat
they ended, thanks to a kind Providence, in accordance with my wishes

readings.title: My poor old grandmother — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how Douglass quotes himself and a poet, and why the older text appears in quotation marks.
readings.focus: A grandmother turned out to die, and a quarrel over a disabled cousin that sends Douglass back to the Eastern Shore.
readings.context: When his old master died, Douglass, about ten, was valued with the estate and fell to Lucretia Auld, who sent him back to Hugh Auld’s family in Baltimore. His grandmother had raised him in her cabin at Tuckahoe. The paragraphs in quotation marks come from his first book, the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845). John Greenleaf Whittier, a Quaker poet, wrote antislavery verse. Uncle Tom is the Christian hero of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852).
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes an old woman turned out to die alone, and a disabled young woman treated as worthless property.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, “The Vicissitudes of Slave Life,” from the death of Mrs. Lucretia to the end of the chapter; opens “One trouble over, and on comes another. The slave's life is full of uncertainty. I had…”; closes “…which plan, and matters connected therewith the kind reader shall learn more hereafter.”.

questions.prompt: In the passage he quotes from his earlier book, what services does Douglass list that his grandmother gave her master? What do they prove?
facilitatorNotes: She rocked him in infancy, served him through life and closed his eyes at death; she “peopled his plantation,” so her children were his wealth. The list proves the “base ingratitude” he charges: the property she produced is kept, and she is discarded once of “little value.”
evidence: She had been the source of all his wealth
they took her to the woods, built her a little hut, put up a little mud-chimney

questions.prompt: Why might Douglass reprint what he wrote “ten years ago” instead of describing it anew?
facilitatorNotes: The 1845 text is testimony already published, and he stands by it. Its present tense (“If my poor old grandmother now lives”) keeps the uncertainty of that time, which is itself evidence of how families were separated. Some readers will think he simply could not improve on it.
evidence: Ten years ago, while speaking of the state of things in our family, after the events just named, I used this language:
If my poor old grandmother now lives, she lives to suffer in utter loneliness

questions.prompt: What do Whittier’s lines and the paragraph after them add to the picture? Does the heightened language strengthen the testimony or weaken it?
facilitatorNotes: The verse gives the fate of the sold children (the rice swamp, the slave-whip); the prose sets the grandmother alone, hearing the dove and the owl, where “the beginning and ending of human existence meet.” The style is the sentimental rhetoric of antislavery writing; some readers find it moving, others prefer the plain facts before it. Both views can cite the text.
evidence: she hears by day the moans of the dove, and by night the screams of the hideous owl
helpless infancy and painful old age combine together

questions.prompt: How does the quarrel over Henny “illustrate the character of southern chivalry”? Why is the phrase ironic?
facilitatorNotes: Henny, burned as a child, is valued like “a horse with a broken leg”; the brothers pass her back and forth and then use Douglass to punish each other. “Chivalry,” a code of honour, turns out to be pettiness at the expense of people with no say.
evidence: of little more value than a horse with a broken leg
As the ground of misunderstanding will serve to illustrate the character of southern chivalry, and humanity, I will relate it.

readings.title: The right to take food — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a moral argument step by step and test where each step depends on the one before.
readings.focus: Hunger in Thomas Auld’s kitchen and Douglass’s case that the enslaved may take what their labor has earned.
readings.context: In March 1833 Douglass, about fifteen, was sent from Baltimore to the village of St. Michael’s on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, to his legal owner, Captain Thomas Auld, and Auld’s second wife, Rowena. Indian corn-meal is coarse ground maize; a peck is a quarter of a bushel. “Bless them in basket and in store” echoes Deuteronomy 28:5. The “heroes of the revolution” are those of the American Revolution.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass argues that a slave who kills his master only imitates the heroes of the Revolution.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Experience in St. Michael’s,” from his new master and mistress to the end of the argument on stealing; opens “But, to my story. It was now more than seven years since I had lived with Master Thomas…”; closes “…experience; albeit, my opinions have, in some sort, been formed by that experience.”.

questions.prompt: How much food did the kitchen receive? How does Douglass let numbers make his case?
facilitatorNotes: Half a bushel of meal a week for eight people, from which the great house took a loaf every morning, leaving less than half a peck each, under half the allowance on Lloyd’s plantation. He invites readers to “judge from the following facts,” so the arithmetic carries the charge of meanness.
evidence: There was, each week, one half bushel of corn-meal brought from the mill
not quite a half a peck of meal per week, apiece

questions.prompt: Explain the argument that taking food from his master was “only a question of removal.” What premise does it borrow from the slaveholder?
facilitatorNotes: If the master owns both the meat and Douglass, moving the meat into Douglass changes nothing about ownership; the strength it gives is spent in the master’s service. The premise is the slaveholder’s own: that Douglass is property. The argument turns that law against the master.
evidence: the taking his meat out of one tub, and putting it into another
At first, he owned it in the tub, and last, he owned it in me.

questions.prompt: How does Douglass extend the right from his master to “others”? What limit does he put on it?
facilitatorNotes: Society at large has joined with Master Thomas to rob him of liberty and wages, so his claims run against all who share in it: “each slave belongs to all; all must, therefore, belong to each.” He limits the claim to “his just earnings” and to slaveholders’ property. Readers can test whether “society at large” is too broad.
evidence: Since each slave belongs to all; all must, therefore, belong to each.
Within the bounds of his just earnings

questions.prompt: “Make a man a slave, and you rob him of moral responsibility.” Does Douglass’s own careful reasoning support or undercut this claim?
facilitatorNotes: He says freedom of choice is the essence of accountability, so the blame for what slavery causes falls on slaveholders. Yet he weighed the matter “closely” and acted from “a clear apprehension of the claims of morality,” which shows a moral agent at work. A defensible reading: he means the slave cannot be held guilty under a law that made him property, not that he has no conscience.
evidence: Freedom of choice is the essence of all accountability.
it was, in my case, the result of a clear apprehension of the claims of morality

readings.title: Master Thomas gets religion — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a scene through a narrator who watches for evidence and will not accept appearances.
readings.focus: A slaveholder by marriage, a camp-meeting conversion, and the test of conversion the enslaved applied.
readings.context: Douglass, about sixteen, is enslaved at St. Michael’s by Captain Thomas Auld, once captain of a sloop (a “bay craft”), now a storekeeper who half-starves the four people in his kitchen. A camp-meeting was an outdoor Methodist revival lasting days, with a fenced “pen” where “mourners” sought conversion. The Methodist Discipline is the church’s book of rules. “Over the left” was period slang meaning “not really”; here it is also literal, since Black listeners were placed behind the preachers. “Incapahle” and “coversion” are misprints in the 1855 printing.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Experience in St. Michael’s,” from Captain Auld’s character through his conversion at the camp-meeting; opens “Bad as slaveholders are, I have seldom met with one so entirely destitute of every…”; closes “…my sins, I have not parted with my sense. I shall hold my slaves, and go to heaven too."”.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Douglass, were slaveholders “by marriage-right” the most exacting, and why did the enslaved despise them most?
facilitatorNotes: Lacking the bearing of a born slaveholder, Auld had the love of domination without consistency, showing cruelty in cowardly, mean ways. Douglass says slaves preferred a bold master even at the risk of being shot: the point is respect for consistency, not approval of either kind.
evidence: He was only a slaveholder by marriage-right
His commands were strong, his enforcement weak.

questions.prompt: Trace the layout of the camp-meeting from the pen outward. Where were the colored people placed, and what does the arrangement say?
facilitatorNotes: Pen and altar, the preachers’ stand, seats, a first circle of stately tents, a second circle, wagons, then cooking fires; Black worshippers stood behind the stand with no seats. The ground plan of a revival reproduces the social order it claims to transcend.
evidence: Behind the preachers' stand, a narrow space was marked out for the use of the colored people.
There were no seats provided for this class of persons

questions.prompt: What evidence does Douglass look for in Master Thomas’s conversion? What does he make of “that tear-drop”?
facilitatorNotes: He watches the red face, the groan and a single tear that seems to ask “which way shall I go?”; its hesitation and loneliness make him doubt the whole thing. His real test is the one every slave applies: a true convert frees his slaves, or at least treats them better.
evidence: The hesitating behavior of that tear-drop, and its loneliness, distressed me
The highest evidence the slaveholder can give the slave of his acceptance with God, is the emancipation of his slaves.

questions.prompt: Set the Methodist rule Douglass quotes beside the speech he imagines from Master Thomas. What do they show about the church?
facilitatorNotes: The rule declares slavery a great evil and bars slaveholders from church office; the imagined speech (“parted with my sins … not parted with my sense”) shows how a convert could keep religion and property apart. The next pages show the rule ignored, but the reader can already see the gap.
evidence: no slaveholder shall be eligible to any official station in our church
I shall hold my slaves, and go to heaven too.

readings.title: The Sabbath school and cousin Henny — excerpt
readings.challenge: Compare what religious men say with what they do, and notice the one exception Douglass names.
readings.focus: Piety that hardened cruelty: the preachers’ home, the mob that broke up a Sunday school, and the whipping of a disabled woman.
readings.context: Douglass, about sixteen, is enslaved at St. Michael’s by Captain Thomas Auld, newly converted at a Methodist camp-meeting. An exhorter is a lay preacher; class-leaders lead small groups of church members. George Cookman was an English-born Methodist minister lost at sea in 1841 aboard the steamship President. “Colonization” was the plan, promoted by the American Colonization Society, to send freed Black Americans to Africa. Henny, Douglass’s cousin, was badly burned as a child and could hardly use her hands. The verse Auld quotes is Luke 12:47.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes the repeated whipping of a disabled young woman, justified with scripture, and a threat to shoot a boy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Experience in St. Michael’s,” from Master Thomas’s new piety to his excuse for holding slaves; opens “Possibly, to convince us that we must not presume too much upon his recent conversion, he…”; closes “…slaveholders have returned to that inquiry, viz: "I hold my slaves for their own good."”.

questions.prompt: What evidence does Douglass give that religion made Master Thomas “more cruel and hateful”?
facilitatorNotes: He grew more rigid in his demands, prayed loudly morning and evening, yet sent no more meal to the kitchen; he fed visiting preachers while starving his slaves (“while he starved us, he stuffed them”). His rise in the church, “as rapid as the growth of the fabled vine of Jack’s bean,” makes the contrast comic and bitter.
evidence: If religion had any effect on his character at all, it made him more cruel and hateful in all his ways.
for while he starved us, he stuffed them

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass single out the Rev. George Cookman? What does the exception prove about the others?
facilitatorNotes: Cookman cared for bodies and souls “alike,” asked about the slaves’ minds and urged slaveholders to free their people. One preacher who could do this shows the others could have; their indifference was chosen. Douglass’s praise is qualified: Cookman mixed antislavery feeling with “colonization ideas.”
evidence: Our souls and our bodies were all alike sacred in his sight
he really had a good deal of genuine anti-slavery feeling mingled with his colonization ideas

questions.prompt: Who broke up the Sabbath school, and what were the children learning? Why does Douglass give the leaders’ church titles?
facilitatorNotes: Two class-leaders and Master Thomas, with sticks, drove off a school teaching children to read the gospel. The titles expose hypocrisy: churchmen attack Bible reading. The threat about Nat Turner shows that literacy itself was feared as the seed of revolt.
evidence: simply teaching a few colored children how to read the gospel of the Son of God
as for my part, I wanted to be another Nat Turner

questions.prompt: How does Auld use scripture against Henny, and how does Douglass answer the claim “I hold my slaves for their own good”?
facilitatorNotes: He whips her and quotes the verse about the servant “beaten with many stripes,” which Douglass calls blasphemy. Then he turns her adrift while keeping the able-bodied, who could have supported themselves in freedom: he frees the one who could not survive and holds the ones who could, the reverse of “their own good.”
evidence: with blood-chilling blasphemy, he would quote the passage of scripture
yet, turning loose the only cripple among them, virtually to starve and die

readings.title: To Covey’s — excerpt
readings.challenge: Hear the narrator retell his whole life as a series of removals, and ask what the pattern means.
readings.focus: Arrival at the farm of a professional “breaker,” and a city boy who has never worked in the fields.
readings.context: Thomas Auld, finding Douglass, now sixteen, unmanageable after his years in Baltimore, has hired him out for 1834 to Edward Covey, a poor farm renter and fellow Methodist with a reputation for “breaking” young slaves, as horses are broken, cheaply, for their owners. Wales are welts.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes a flogging and the language of “breaking” people like animals.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “Covey, the Negro Breaker,” from the journey to the farm to the first flogging; opens “THE morning of the first of January, 1834, with its chilling wind and pinching frost,…”; closes “…with him. But, here are the facts connected with the affair, precisely as they occurred.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass retells his life in one long sentence of removals. List the stages. What do the verbs say about who acts?
facilitatorNotes: Grandmother’s cabin, old master’s, Baltimore, the Eastern Shore valuation, Baltimore again, St. Michael’s, now Covey’s. The verbs are passive or done to him (“snatched,” “hurried away,” “removed,” “sent”); his only act is walking where he is ordered. The sentence ends with being “broken to the yoke.”
evidence: I am ruthlessly snatched from the hearth of a fond grandmother
I am to be broken to the yoke of a bitter and life-long bondage

questions.prompt: How do the weather and the view of the bay match his state of mind?
facilitatorNotes: The cold wind and frost are “in harmony with the winter in my own mind”; the foaming bay, black pines and desert-like shore make the place “wild and desolate.” The landscape becomes an image of what awaits him.
evidence: quite in harmony with the winter in my own mind
deepened the wild and desolate aspect of my new home

questions.prompt: Douglass’s “only consolation” was the certainty of finding Covey as cruel as reported. Why could certainty console?
facilitatorNotes: After a life of sudden removals, uncertainty itself was a torment (compare the valuation). Knowing the worst lets him prepare. The line is also grimly ironic: comfort is reduced to accurate expectation of cruelty.
evidence: the certainty of finding him precisely as represented by common fame

questions.prompt: Why call Covey “my brother in the Methodist church” in the sentence about the first beating? What does Douglass think Covey intended?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase is ironic: church brotherhood means nothing against ownership. Douglass supposes Covey wanted to establish their relation by blows at once, since he had only a year to “complete his work.” The beating is presented as method, not temper.
evidence: my brother in the Methodist church
since he had but a single year in which to complete his work, the sooner he began, the better

readings.title: The unbroken oxen — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a fast narrative and notice where Douglass stops it to draw a comparison.
readings.focus: The oxen, the gate and the goads: a lesson in being broken.
readings.context: Recap: on 1 January 1834 Douglass, sixteen, walked to the farm of Edward Covey, a renter famed for “breaking” young slaves, to work for a year as a field hand for the first time; within three days Covey flogged him, and Douglass promised to tell why. “Woa,” “back,” “gee” and “hither” are commands to draft animals; the “in hand” and “off hand” oxen are the two of a yoked pair; goads are sticks for driving cattle.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes a flogging with sticks after Covey strips Douglass by force.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “Covey, the Negro Breaker,” the ox-cart in the woods and the flogging that followed; opens “On one of the coldest days of the whole month of January, 1834, I was ordered, at day…”; closes “…many which came after it, and these, for offenses far lighter than the gate breaking.”.

questions.prompt: Why was Covey’s order “about as unreasonable, as a command to shoulder a mad bull”? List what made the task impossible.
facilitatorNotes: Unbroken oxen, no instruction beyond their names and a few commands, a rope tied to the horns, and a driver who had never handled cattle. Douglass later learns that even Covey would not have taken such oxen into the woods without first training them in the open field, so the task looks like a setup.
evidence: this order was about as unreasonable, as a command to shoulder a mad bull!
even Covey himself would not have undertaken

questions.prompt: Which animal images does Douglass attach to Covey in his portrait, and how do they prepare what follows?
facilitatorNotes: A “wolfish visage,” a growl “like a dog” guarding a bone; later he rushes “with something of the savage fierceness of a wolf.” In a chapter about breaking animals, the breaker is the beast.
evidence: of thin and wolfish visage
like a dog, when an attempt is made to take a bone from him

questions.prompt: “They were property, so was I; they were to be broken, so was I.” What does this short paragraph do in the middle of the story?
facilitatorNotes: It halts the action to state the parallel in balanced clauses: Douglass is breaking oxen while being broken himself. “Break and be broken--such is life” turns the scene into an image of the whole system, in which each is forced to master someone below.
evidence: They were property, so was I; they were to be broken, so was I.
Covey was to break me, I was to break them

questions.prompt: Douglass refuses to undress: “If you will beat me, you shall do so over my clothes.” What does the refusal show, given that Covey still strips him?
facilitatorNotes: It is a first, small resistance, a claim of dignity even when it fails. It foreshadows a larger refusal; this flogging, he says, was only “the first of a series.” Readers may ask what it cost him and why he records it.
evidence: To this unreasonable order I made no reply, but sternly refused to take off my clothing.
This flogging was the first of a series of floggings

readings.title: “The snake” — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Douglass reports about Covey from the general conclusions he draws about slavery.
readings.focus: Surveillance, sham piety, and a woman bought “as a breeder.”
readings.context: Douglass, sixteen, spent 1834 hired out to Edward Covey, a farm renter famed for “breaking” young slaves, who flogged him in his first days for wrecking a cart with unbroken oxen. “Like a very Turk” is a period stereotype for furious energy. To raise a hymn is to start the singing. “Extatic” is the printing’s spelling.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes the sexual coercion of an enslaved woman bought “as a breeder,” in Douglass’s period terms.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “Covey, the Negro Breaker,” from Covey’s methods of work to the purchase of Caroline; opens “I remained with Mr. Covey one year, (I cannot say I lived with him,) and during the first…”; closes “…with a view to increasing the number and quality of the former, as of the latter.”.

questions.prompt: How did Covey make his workers feel that “he was always present”? Find two of his tricks.
facilitatorNotes: He crept through ditches and gullies, pretended to ride to St. Michael’s and then lay flat in a ditch, and gave orders as if leaving for days before doubling back. The effect was constant fear: “We were never secure.”
evidence: He had the faculty of making us feel that he was always present.
the snake-like Covey lying flat in the ditch

questions.prompt: Douglass explains these tricks by the system and also by the man. How do the two explanations fit together?
facilitatorNotes: Slavery gives no motive to work but fear, so a master assumes idleness whenever fear is absent and invents deceptions to keep it alive. But “with Mr. Covey, trickery was natural,” and it shaped even his prayers. The system rewards a character like his; it does not excuse it.
evidence: The fear of punishment is the sole motive for any sort of industry, with him.
But, with Mr. Covey, trickery was natural.

questions.prompt: What does the story of Caroline show about how a poor man built a fortune in a slave state?
facilitatorNotes: Owning people was “the first condition of wealth and respectability”; Covey could afford one woman and bought her to bear children, compelling her and locking her up with the hired man. Her twins are an “addition to his human stock,” counted as increase. Douglass names her, which the system did not.
evidence: The first condition of wealth and respectability there, being the ownership of human property
At this addition to his human stock

questions.prompt: Douglass predicts the story will be read with disgust in the North and laughed at in the South. Why bring in both audiences? Is the claim fair?
facilitatorNotes: He writes for northern readers and wants them to see that the law and custom of slave states treated a woman like breeding stock. The prediction is a generalisation; some readers will think it too broad, others that the comparison with “buying a cow” is exactly what the law permitted. Ask what evidence would settle it.
evidence: while this fact will be read with disgust and shame at the north, it will be laughed at
than for buying a cow, and raising stock from her

readings.title: The ships on the Chesapeake — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read an apostrophe, a speech to something that cannot answer, and follow the turns of feeling inside it.
readings.focus: Douglass broken in body and spirit, and ships that turn despair into a plan.
readings.context: Douglass, sixteen, spent the first months of 1834 hired out to Edward Covey, a farmer on the Chesapeake Bay famed for “breaking” young slaves, who worked and flogged him without let-up. Most of this passage is quoted from his first book, the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845). Ague is a fever with fits of shivering.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass describes thoughts of taking his own life and Covey’s.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “Covey, the Negro Breaker,” the passage quoted from his first book and the end of the chapter; opens “I will here reproduce what I said of my own experience in this wretched place, more than…”; closes “…hope for freedom"--rendered me a living embodiment of mental and physical wretchedness.”.

questions.prompt: “Mr. Covey succeeded in breaking me.” What does Douglass say was lost?
facilitatorNotes: Body, soul and spirit: his elasticity, his intellect, the wish to read, the spark in his eye. The paragraph ends “behold a man transformed into a brute!”, reversing the slaveholders’ claim: a man is made a brute by slavery, not born one.
evidence: I was broken in body, soul and spirit.
the disposition to read departed

questions.prompt: Why are the sails, “so delightful to the eye of freemen,” “shrouded ghosts” to him?
facilitatorNotes: The same sight means opposite things depending on who sees it. White sails become shrouds because each ship leaving for the ocean reminds him of the freedom he lacks.
evidence: so delightful to the eye of freemen
were to me so many shrouded ghosts, to terrify and torment me

questions.prompt: Trace the turns in the speech to the ships. Where does lament become a question, and where does the question become a plan?
facilitatorNotes: It opens with contrasts (loosed and free, fast in chains), rises to “O, that I were free!”, then doubts (“Is there any God? Why am I a slave?”), then resolves (“I will run away”) and works out a route by water and through Delaware. It ends by consoling himself to wait. The speech enacts a mind moving from despair to purpose.
evidence: Is there any God? Why am I a slave? I will run away.
I will take to the water.

questions.prompt: The speech ends “There is a better day coming.” How do the chapter’s last two paragraphs complicate that hope?
facilitatorNotes: Back in the present he describes swinging between near madness and resignation, haunted by the thought of being “a slave for life” with “no rational ground to hope.” The hope is unstable. Readers who know what follows may argue the ending prepares a turn; others will stress how near he came to giving up.
evidence: goaded almost to madness at one time, and at another reconciling myself to my wretched condition
a slave with no rational ground to hope for freedom

readings.title: Struck down in the treading yard — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how Douglass addresses the reader and asks us to imagine passing by.
readings.focus: Collapse from heat, Covey’s kick and blow, and a desperate walk to appeal to his master.
readings.context: Douglass, sixteen, has spent half of 1834 hired out to Edward Covey, a farmer famed for “breaking” young slaves, who worked and flogged him until he felt “broken in body, soul and spirit.” In a treading yard horses trample out the wheat; the fan, a hand-cranked winnowing machine, blows away the chaff. His owner, Thomas Auld, keeps a store seven miles away in St. Michael’s; Douglass calls Covey Auld’s “brother” as a fellow Methodist.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Describes the beating of a sick young man, a head wound and heavy bleeding.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Another Pressure of the Tyrant’s Vice,” from the opening to his resolve to appeal to his master; opens “THE foregoing chapter, with all its horrid incidents and shocking features, may be taken…”; closes “…and defaced; and I will go to him, and tell him the simple truth about the matter."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass narrate this change “although I may seem thereby to applaud my own courage”? What does he want it to show?
facilitatorNotes: He offers it as evidence of “human nature, when subjected to the terrible extremities of slavery,” not as a boast. Having shown how he was broken, he will now show “the converse,” how a broken man recovers. The story is framed as an argument.
evidence: help the reader to a better understanding of human nature
now let us see the converse of all this

questions.prompt: Why did Douglass’s collapse bring “the entire work to a dead stand”? What does this detail add?
facilitatorNotes: The four workers depended on one another, so the fan stopped when he fell, and Covey heard it. The detail shows how closely the work was timed and watched, and that the system depended on the strength of the boy it was crushing.
evidence: each part depended on the other, so that when one stopped, all were compelled to stop

questions.prompt: Douglass says the wound was “fortunate for me.” Why include this strange turn?
facilitatorNotes: Bleeding (a common remedy then) relieved the rush of blood to his head and let him rise. It is dark irony set against Covey’s taunt, and honest about chance. It also keeps the narrator from simple self-pity.
evidence: If you have got the headache, I'll cure you.
Bleeding was never more efficacious.

questions.prompt: What argument does Douglass expect will move Thomas Auld, and what does his choice reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Not humanity, which he doubts, but Auld’s interest in his own property: he cannot let it be “bruised and battered.” Douglass reasons inside the slaveholder’s logic because it is the only appeal that might work, which is itself a judgment on Auld.
evidence: if not animated by motives of humanity, he might be induced to interfere on my behalf from selfish considerations
allow his property to be thus bruised and battered, marred and defaced

readings.title: Master Thomas sends him back — excerpt
readings.challenge: Watch a man’s feelings change in a single interview and decide what defeated his first response.
readings.focus: An appeal for protection: humanity that rises in a slaveholder, then falls before the slave system.
readings.context: Recap: in August 1834, collapsing from heat on Edward Covey’s farm, Douglass, sixteen, was kicked and gashed on the head; bleeding, he resolved to walk the seven miles to St. Michael’s and ask his owner, Thomas Auld, who had hired him to Covey for the year, for protection. Epsom salts were a common purgative. The words Douglass turns against slaveholders at the end are Jesus’s about the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23:4).
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Another Pressure of the Tyrant’s Vice,” from his flight toward St. Michael’s to the end of the chapter; opens “In order to get to St. Michael's, by the most favorable and direct road, I must walk…”; closes “…disenthrallment from the tyranny of Covey, and the marked change which it brought about.”.

questions.prompt: What did Douglass see in Master Thomas at first, and how did it disappear?
facilitatorNotes: Auld seemed affected; Douglass saw “his human nature asserting its conviction against the slave system.” Then he paced, found excuses for Covey, justified him fully and condemned Douglass. The movement is from feeling to self-interest, and Douglass names the cause: the system, not only the man.
evidence: I distinctly saw his human nature asserting its conviction against the slave system
humanity fell before the systematic tyranny of slavery

questions.prompt: “The guilt of a slave is always, and everywhere, presumed.” How does the interview prove the claim?
facilitatorNotes: Auld decides without evidence that Douglass deserved the flogging and was faking; Douglass cannot even deny it, since denial would be “impudence.” The slave has no standing to give testimony against a white man.
evidence: My dizziness was laziness, and Covey did right to flog me, as he had done.
is a final silencer of counter statements from the lips of a slave

questions.prompt: What was “the most distressing thought of all” to Master Thomas? What does it reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Losing a year’s wages if Douglass left Covey. Money outweighs the fear that Covey will kill him, which Auld dismisses as nonsense. His “brother in the church” is protected; his property must return.
evidence: and this I found was the most distressing thought of all to him
I should lose your wages for the entire year

questions.prompt: In the last paragraphs Douglass turns the charge of laziness back on slaveholders. Is the reply fair? Why use Jesus’s words?
facilitatorNotes: He argues that Auld imagines what he would do in a slave’s place, and that slaveholders, who dread labor, use the charge as “the standing apology” for cruelty. It is a generalisation, but it rests on the scene just told. The scripture answers men who quote scripture to justify whipping.
evidence: The charge of laziness against the slaves is ever on their lips
bind heavy burdens, grievous to be borne

readings.title: A night in the woods, and Sandy — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice the shift into the present tense and what it does to the scene in the woods.
readings.focus: Despair, hiding from Covey, and the kindness of Sandy and his wife.
readings.context: In August 1834 Douglass, sixteen, fled to his owner, Thomas Auld, after the farmer Edward Covey, to whom he was hired for the year, kicked him and cut his head open when he collapsed from heat. Auld refused to protect him and ordered him back. Thirty-nine lashes was a common legal punishment; an ash cake is cornmeal dough baked in the ashes of a fire. The “lord mayors and aldermen, over the sea” are from his lecture tour of Britain and Ireland (1845–47).
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass describes despair and a man taken in chains to be sold south.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “The Last Flogging,” from his sleepless night to the supper at Sandy’s; opens “SLEEP itself does not always come to the relief of the weary in body, and the broken in…”; closes “…was the meal, of all my life, most sweet to my taste, and now most vivid in my memory.”.

questions.prompt: “My master … had even now refused to protect me as his property.” Explain the two kinds of protection Douglass had hoped for.
facilitatorNotes: He never hoped Auld would protect him as a man, out of humanity; he did hope Auld would protect him as property, out of self-interest. Auld refused even that, so “the last hope had been extinguished.”
evidence: My master, who I did not venture to hope would protect me as a man, had even now refused to protect me as his property
The last hope had been extinguished.

questions.prompt: Douglass shifts into the present tense: “Well, now I am clear of Covey.” What does the shift do, and what choice does he face?
facilitatorNotes: It puts us in the woods with him. His choice is to stay and starve or go back and be torn by the lash: “the painful alternative.” He would have exchanged “manhood for the brutehood of an ox,” echoing the oxen of the earlier chapter.
evidence: This was the painful alternative presented to me.
I would have exchanged my manhood for the brutehood of an ox

questions.prompt: Why could Douglass not pray in the woods, though “Covey could pray--Capt. Auld could pray”?
facilitatorNotes: The “sham religion” of slaveholders had cast doubt on all religion and made prayer seem “unavailing and delusive.” The boy who once prayed with Father Lawson now finds his faith damaged by the men who pray most loudly.
evidence: But how could I pray?
the sham religion which everywhere prevailed

questions.prompt: What risks did Sandy and his wife take, and why does Douglass call the ash cake “the meal, of all my life, most sweet”?
facilitatorNotes: Sheltering a runaway could cost thirty-nine lashes or worse; the house belonged to Sandy’s free wife. They fed him because he was loved for his knowledge (the only other reader nearby, Jim, had been sold south). Set against later feasts with lord mayors, the poor supper is sweeter because of who gave it and when.
evidence: he would have suffered the penalty of thirty-nine lashes on his bare back
was the meal, of all my life, most sweet to my taste

readings.title: Sandy’s root — excerpt
readings.challenge: Weigh how much Douglass credits Sandy’s root, and notice how he leaves the question open.
readings.focus: Folk belief, insight and resolve: the root, Covey’s Sunday face, and the decision to resist.
readings.context: Recap: sent back to the farmer Edward Covey by his owner after a beating, Douglass, sixteen, hid in the woods all Saturday; that night Sandy, an enslaved man on his way to his free wife’s house, took him in and fed him. Potpie Neck is a narrow neck of land near St. Michael’s. To “backslide” is to fall away from religious commitment.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Douglass describes Sandy’s African folk belief in period terms (“a genuine African,” “superstition”).

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “The Last Flogging,” from the council with Sandy to Monday morning; opens “Supper over, Sandy and I went into a discussion of what was possible for me, under the…”; closes “…and I soon had occasion to make my fallen state known to my Sunday-pious brother, Covey.”.

questions.prompt: Why was running away impossible from where Douglass stood?
facilitatorNotes: He was on a narrow neck of land with the bay on one side and Pot-pie river on the other; the only way out led past St. Michael’s, where he would be seen. Geography, not courage, decided it.
evidence: I was on a narrow neck of land, every avenue from which would bring me in sight of pursuers

questions.prompt: What argument of Sandy’s won Douglass over, and what does Douglass think of the root?
facilitatorNotes: Sandy points out that book learning “had not kept Covey off me,” a hard answer to the proud reader. Douglass thinks the root absurd, even sinful, and takes it “to please him”; yet he respects Sandy’s “insight into human nature.” He separates the man’s wisdom from his belief.
evidence: had not kept Covey off me
I saw in Sandy too deep an insight into human nature, with all his superstition

questions.prompt: How does Douglass explain Covey’s Sunday manner? Is the joke about “breaking the Sabbath” fair?
facilitatorNotes: He suspects the Sabbath, not the root: Covey would not work or whip on Sunday but would on Monday. The pun on “breaking” sums up a religion that respects “the day” more than “the man for whom the day was mercifully given.”
evidence: I suspected, however, that the Sabbath, and not the root, was the real explanation of Covey's manner.
His religion hindered him from breaking the Sabbath, but not from breaking my skin.

questions.prompt: What did Douglass resolve on Sunday, and why does he call it having “backslidden”?
facilitatorNotes: To obey every order but, if beaten, to defend himself. He had been taught that resisting a master was against religion; Auld’s indifference “severed the last link.” Calling it backsliding is ironic: in the slaveholders’ creed it is a fall, in the book’s argument it is the start of recovery.
evidence: to obey every order, however unreasonable, if it were possible
Master Thomas's indifference had severed the last link.

readings.title: The fight with Covey — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a physical struggle closely and track who is defending and who attacking at each stage.
readings.focus: Resistance without retaliation, and three others who will not obey Covey.
readings.context: Recap: Douglass, sixteen, was sent back to Edward Covey, the farmer hired to “break” him, after appealing to his owner; he hid in the woods, where his friend Sandy gave him a root said to stop any white man from whipping him. On Sunday Covey was mild, and Douglass resolved to obey every order but defend himself if attacked. Hughes is Covey’s cousin; Bill Smith is hired from another owner; Caroline is enslaved by Covey. Blades are corn leaves kept as fodder.
readings.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement and the racist beliefs that upheld it; its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A violent fight; Covey strikes Caroline for refusing to help him; Bill’s speech is given in dialect.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “The Last Flogging,” from Covey’s attack in the stable to his giving up the contest; opens “Whilst I was obeying his order to feed and get the horses ready for the field, and when…”; closes “…victorious, because my aim had not been to injure him, but to prevent his injuring me.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass says he “was strictly on the defensive.” When does that change, and why?
facilitatorNotes: When Hughes joins in, he gives blows as well, “aggressive toward Hughes” while still only holding Covey. The proverb about being hanged for a sheep explains it: since he will suffer for resisting anyway, he may as well resist fully.
evidence: I was strictly on the defensive
I was still defensive toward Covey, but aggressive toward Hughes

questions.prompt: “The very color of the man was forgotten.” What does this suggest about how slavery had worked on Douglass’s mind until then?
facilitatorNotes: Color had been a barrier of fear backed by law; in the fight he acts “as though we stood as equals before the law.” Forgetting it means the fear itself was learned and could be broken.
evidence: as heedless of consequences, at the moment, as though we stood as equals before the law
The very color of the man was forgotten.

questions.prompt: Compare Bill’s refusal with Caroline’s. Why does Douglass say that “in her, it was at greater peril”?
facilitatorNotes: Bill was hired, and his owner forbade beatings; he can say he was hired to work, not to whip. Caroline belonged to Covey, who could do what he pleased with her, and she was struck. “We were all in open rebellion, that morning”: Douglass gives the others their share of the victory.
evidence: My master hired me here, to work, and not to help you whip Frederick.
she was the slave of Covey, and he could do what he pleased with her

questions.prompt: Covey says he would not have whipped Douglass “half so much” had he not resisted. What is wrong with the claim, and why might he make it?
facilitatorNotes: He had not whipped him at all or drawn a drop of blood; the words save face. Douglass counts himself the victor because his aim was only to prevent injury. The gap between claim and fact matters in the next pages.
evidence: The fact was, he had not whipped me at all.
my aim had not been to injure him, but to prevent his injuring me

readings.title: “I was a man now” — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a narrator’s interpretation of an event and test it against the event as told.
readings.focus: The fight as the turning point: force, dignity, and a freedom of spirit before freedom in law.
readings.context: Recap: in August 1834 Douglass, sixteen, fought off Edward Covey, the farmer hired to “break” him, for two hours in the stable and cow yard; two other workers refused to help Covey, who finally gave up and claimed he had whipped him. The closing lines are from Lord Byron’s poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, about Greeks under foreign rule.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “The Last Flogging,” from the months after the fight to the end of the chapter; opens “During the whole six months that I lived with Covey, after this transaction, he never…”; closes “"Hereditary bondmen, know ye not Who would be free, themselves must strike the blow?"”.

questions.prompt: List what the fight “rekindled” or “recalled to life” in Douglass.
facilitatorNotes: The embers of liberty, his Baltimore dreams, his sense of manhood, self-respect and self-confidence, and a determination to be free. The capitals (“I WAS A MAN NOW”) mark the turn as the centre of the book.
evidence: It rekindled in my breast the smouldering embers of liberty
I was nothing before; I WAS A MAN NOW.

questions.prompt: “A man, without force, is without the essential dignity of humanity.” Do you agree? How does the next sentence qualify it?
facilitatorNotes: He explains that human nature “cannot honor a helpless man, although it can pity him”: the claim is about how others regard the powerless. Many readers will push back that dignity does not depend on force, and his own earlier chapters show dignity in the helpless; others will say he describes the world as it treats people, not as it should.
evidence: Human nature is so constituted, that it cannot honor a helpless man, although it can pity him

questions.prompt: “This spirit made me a freeman in fact, while I remained a slave in form.” Explain the paradox.
facilitatorNotes: Legally nothing changed, but a master’s power rests on fear of the lash and of death; once he was “not afraid to die,” that power was broken. “When a slave cannot be flogged he is more than half free.”
evidence: I had reached the point, at which I was not afraid to die.
When a slave cannot be flogged he is more than half free.

questions.prompt: Why, by Douglass’s explanation, did Covey not have him punished by law? What does it show about reputation?
facilitatorNotes: Covey’s business as a “negro breaker” depended on his name; admitting he had been beaten by a boy of sixteen would ruin it. Interest and pride kept him silent. Douglass also admits he later tried to provoke a second fight, an honest note against his own heroism.
evidence: Covey was, probably, ashamed to have it known and confessed that he had been mastered by a boy of sixteen
His interest and his pride mutually suggested the wisdom of passing the matter by, in silence.
